articles.title: VP Trial Day 21: Defense lawyer Michael Poa to testify in impeachment court
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte’s defense counsel and former Department of Education (DepEd) Chief of Staff Michael Poa is scheduled to testify on Wednesday, September 2. He will be…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte’s defense counsel and former Department of Education (DepEd) Chief of Staff Michael Poa is scheduled to testify on Wednesday, September 2.
He will be called on by the prosecution panel to take the witness stand.
The counsel cannot yet be called a hostile witness at this time, since this description comes after he has been formally presented by the prosecution to the impeachment court.

Poa is expected to testify about the DepEd’s use of confidential funds (CFs) when Duterte was its secretary from 2022 to 2024.During that period, while Poa was the secretary’s chief of staff, the department disbursed P112.5 million in CFs.
Among these disbursements are P15 million supposedly used to help fund the Armed Forces of the Philippines Youth Leadership Summits.
Poa had supposedly requested military certification for after the Commission on Audit required supporting documents to explain how DepEd used its CFs.
Over the weekend, House Deputy Speaker Paolo Ortega V called Poa a “central figure” in Duterte’s impeachment, especially as he served as both Duterte’s chief of staff and spokesperson at DepEd.
The lawmaker noted that it was likely that Poa knew how the confidential funds were processed within the agency at that time as part of his job.
After his role at DepEd, Poa continued to represent Duterte as counsel as early as the first impeachment complaints were filed against the vice president in 2025.
Poa’s testimony will then be followed by Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) Assistant National Statistician Marizza Grande.

Grande is set to testify on the findings of PSA on the identities of the curious names that appear in the acknowledgment receipts filed by the Office of the Vice President and DepEd as proof of payment for confidential activities. /apl

articles.title: Jinggoy Estrada to pursue legal remedies after Bonoan dropped as co-accused in flood control case
articles.summary: Senator Jinggoy Estrada said he will pursue all available legal remedies after the Sandiganbayan Fifth Division granted the Ombudsman"s motion to drop former Public Works Secretary Manuel Bonoan as a…

blocks.text: Published September 2, 2026 7:27am

Senator Jinggoy Estrada said he will pursue all available legal remedies after the Sandiganbayan Fifth Division granted the Ombudsman’s motion to drop former Public Works Secretary Manuel Bonoan as a co-accused in the plunder and graft case involving the senator.
In a statement on Tuesday, Estrada said he respected the court’s decision but pointed out that such development did not end his legal recourse.

“While I respect the decision of the Sandiganbayan, I wish to emphasize that there remain legal remedies available to me under our judicial system, which my legal team will carefully study and pursue at the appropriate time,” Estrada said.
“I intend to avail myself of all remedies provided under our laws,” he added.
Estrada also said he would continue to rely on due process and the rule of law.
“My faith in our judicial system remains firm. I will continue to stand by the truth and pursue every lawful means available to protect my rights and clear my name and honor,” he said.
The Sandiganbayan Fifth Division, voting 2-1, ruled that it was within the Ombudsman’s “prosecutorial discretion” to determine which accused it would use as a state witness.

“The decision to move for the discharge of an accused is part of the Ombudsman’s prosecutorial discretion of who should be used as a state witness, to bolster the successful prosecution of criminal offenses,” the court said based on a copy of the decision obtained by GMA News.
Bonoan was among Estrada’s co-accused in the case, along with three others.
The Ombudsman charged them in May for allegedly conspiring to amass more than P500 million in kickbacks from flood control projects.
In June, the Ombudsman asked the Sandiganbayan to exclude Bonoan from the charges after the former Department of Public Works and Highways chief expressed willingness to cooperate with the agency.
The Ombudsman said Bonoan’s testimony was necessary to uncover the alleged system behind the kickback scheme involving anomalous flood control projects.
“His cooperation was indispensable to uncover the architecture that may have set the entire machinery in motion,” the Ombudsman said in its June 11, 2026 resolution.
The Sandiganbayan also said the Ombudsman is empowered under the law to grant immunity to a state witness.
Estrada and Bonoan have yet to be arraigned by the Sandiganbayan Fifth Division due to pending motions. The court has scheduled Estrada’s arraignment for September 3. —KG, GMA News

articles.summary: The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte continues on Tuesday, September 2, 2026. Here are the latest news and updates.

blocks.text: Published September 2, 2026 7:11am
Atty. Michael Poa, spokesperson for the defense panel, will take the witness stand today, September 2, 2026. Senate/File
Sara Duterte impeachment trial Day 21: What to expect
A familiar face from the defense team of Vice President Sara Duterte will be called to the witness stand on Wednesday to address allegations of the misuse of confidential funds.
Michael Poa, spokesperson for the defense panel, will be presented by the House prosecution team as its next witness in the trial.
He is expected to testify on how the Department of Education (DepEd) disbursed P112.5 million in confidential funds during Duterte's tenure as Education secretary.
Poa served as DepEd chief of staff and spokesperson when the agency was still under Duterte's leadership.
On Tuesday, lawyer Justin Nicol Gular said that Poa temporarily stepped out of his role as the defense spokesperson amid his status as a witness.

Aside from Poa, the prosecution also requested the Senate impeachment court to issue a subpoena for Marizza Grande of the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) to compel her to attend Wednesday’s trial.

Grande will be called in as a witness after the testimony of Poa. Like any other witnesses, both of them will face direct and cross-examinations from the prosecution and defense panels, respectively, as well as interjections from the senator-judges.

Their testimonies will still be in relation to Article 1 of the impeachment case, which accuses the Vice President of committing impeachable offenses due to systematic misappropriation and irregular liquidation of confidential funds amounting to P500 million released to the Office of the Vice President (OVP) and P112.5 million released to the DepEd. —Giselle Ombay/LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Fund defence spending from tax rise on middle earners, thinktank tells Healey
articles.summary:
Resolution Foundation argues that UK’s internationally low ‘tax wedge’ must rise to pay for defence ambitions

The chancellor, John Healey, must be prepared to raise taxes for middle earners…

blocks.text: The chancellor, John Healey, must be prepared to raise taxes for middle earners if he wants to fund significantly higher defence spending, the Resolution Foundation thinktank has said.
Healey resigned from Keir Starmer’s government in June, protesting against what he argued was the then prime minister’s failure to adequately fund defence.

But in his new post in No 11 Downing Street, Healey has made clear that he will wait until next year’s spending review before presenting a plan to meet Labour’s pledge of devoting 3.5% of GDP to defence by 2035.

In a new report, entitled Thin End of the Wedge, economists at the Resolution Foundation suggest he will not be able to raise the £28bn a year it would take to meet that promise without asking average workers to pay more.

They say that despite historically large tax rises since Labour came to power in 2024, amounting to £70bn a year, the “tax wedge” – taxes on earnings, minus benefits – remains low by international standards.
“Despite recent increases, the UK still taxes average earners less than most of our international peers,” says the foundation’s chief economist, James Smith.

The analysis shows that tax rises under Healey’s predecessor, Rachel Reeves, resulted in a 2.4 percentage point jump in the tax wedge last year – the largest for any country in the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD).
Yet at 32.4% for a single earner on average pay, it remains below the average for the OECD and the G7 major economies, they say.

When the economists looked at countries with higher public spending, they found these tended to ask their average workers to contribute more – instead of relying on business or wealth taxes, for example.
“No other OECD rich country has a bigger state and a lower burden on average workers, so any politician promising both is not being realistic,” Smith said.
“There is a strong case that any benefits of increased defence spending will be broadly shared, so the tax rises needed to find this should be too, including higher rates on middle earners.”
after newsletter promotion

The tax wedge on a worker paid the median salary, of £33,000 as at April last year, is also low by historic standards, they argue – and is still below the level before the global financial crisis in 2008.

In Reeves’s two tax-raising budgets before she was sacked by Andy Burnham, the biggest revenue-raisers were employer national insurance contributions and fiscal drag – where income tax thresholds were left unchanged, so that more people end up paying higher rates.
She was constrained by Labour’s pre-election promise not to increase the rates of income tax, VAT or employee national insurance – which Burnham has promised to stick to.

As well as the longer-term defence pledge, Burnham’s government faces pressure to do more to cushion households against rising energy bills over the coming winter, and to beef up efforts to help unemployed young people into work.

Healey will present his first budget on 28 October and needs to find approximately £1.4bn a year over the next three years to pay for Starmer’s defence investment plan – which Healey in his last job derided as inadequate.

articles.title: No confidential intel behind DepEd-backed youth summits, says Army officer
articles.summary: An Army officer says DepEd gave only open-source information for military youth programs.

blocks.text: September 2, 2026 | 7:00am
Colonel Manaros Boransing speaks during the the Senate Impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on Tuesday, Sept. 1, 2026.
Senate PRIB

MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Education did not provide confidential or surveillance information to the military for its Youth Leadership Summits, said a military officer whose certification was later used to support DepEd's questioned confidential fund expenses.

Col. Manaros Boransing II testified at the Senate impeachment court Tuesday, September 1, suggesting that the P15.54 million spending the Commission on Audit flagged was not used for activity for which they were cited.
During interpellation by Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian, Boransing said DepEd provided only open-source information about students who could participate in the summits.

"For the First Infantry Tabak Division? No, sir, they did not provide any confidential or surveillance information," Boransing said, partly in Filipino. "What they give is open-source information about their students."
Boransing had even said he did not know his certification would be used as an excuse for the expenses.

DepEd's involvement was limited to sharing basic, non-classified details, such as identifying potential student leaders who could participate in the summits and determining which school facilities were available and safe to host the events, he said.

Gatchalian further pressed Boransing on whether DepEd had ever provided confidential or surveillance information for these activities in the past, prior to the controversial 2022 and 2023 allocations.

Boransing reiterated that the Armed Forces of the Philippines relies on its own intelligence units to identify security threats and crucial locations, rather than receiving confidential information from civilian agencies such as DepEd.
"The AFP intelligence units are in charge of gathering information or receiving information... It is not the civil-military operations personnel," Boransing explained.
Boransing served as assistant chief of staff for civil-military operations, G7, of the 1st Infantry "Tabak" Division from 2021 to 2026, during which he helped oversee the YLS.
Why it matters
COA had previously flagged P75 million of DepEd's confidential fund expenses under Vice President Sara Duterte due to a lack of supporting documents.
DepEd later presented military certification letters to support P15.54 million in confidential fund expenses that state auditors had questioned.

Boransing was among the military officials who issued the certifications. However, he said he was unaware that his certification would be used to justify DepEd's confidential fund expenses before COA.

Tuesday marked the 20th day of Duterte's impeachment trial. The Senate impeachment court is currently hearing Article I of the Articles of Impeachment, which concerns allegations over the use of confidential funds by DepEd and the Office of the Vice President.

articles.title: Trump homeland security chief says ICE agents could be sent to polling places
articles.summary:
Markwayne Mullin says officers could be deployed ‘if there is a threat to that polling place or we’re serving a warrant’

US homeland security secretary Markwayne Mullin on Tuesday said that…

blocks.text: US homeland security secretary Markwayne Mullin on Tuesday said that federal immigration and customs enforcement (ICE) officers could be deployed to polling sites across the country.
Speaking to reporters in New York, Mullin said: “ICE isn’t there to patrol the polling places. We’re there to enforce specific threats.”

For months, Democrats and voting rights groups have warned that the Trump administration might attempt to deploy federal agents to polling locations in an effort to intimidate voters and depress turnout ahead of the November midterm elections.
Although the White House has downplayed such suggestions, Donald Trump has declined to rule it out while continuing to sow doubt about the integrity of past – and future – US elections.

“The only reason why we would be at polling places is if there is a threat to that polling place or we’re serving a warrant on someone that we have been actively tracking down,” Mullin said. “ICE’s job is immigration, customs enforcement. That’s their job … if we’re serving a warrant we will be where we need to be.”
Federal law prohibits military personnel or other “armed” agents from being “at any place where a general or special election is held”.

In a separate statement to Politico, the homeland security department said: “ICE is not planning operations targeting polling locations. ICE conducts intelligence-driven targeted enforcement, and if an active public safety threat endangered a polling location, they may be arrested as a result of that targeted enforcement action.”
The Guardian has contacted the DHS for additional comment.

Mullin’s latest comments follow statements he made in July, when he threatened to withhold federal aid from states that refused to comply with homeland security election directives as part of the administration’s crackdown on what it alleges is widespread voter fraud.

“We will scrub all election records, looking for illegal aliens and those who are ineligible to vote, including those that somehow voted, yet they were deceased,” Mullin said earlier this summer, adding: “If states want the grant funding, to recap, they must secure the election.”

Yet experts say the administration has failed to offer any proof for its claims of non-citizen voting. In one instance, DHS officials claimed that there may have been as many as 16,000 non-citizens registered to vote in Nevada, but later admitted they could confirm that only 185 of those people were actually non-citizens, according to records obtained by the Guardian.

Meanwhile, Dan Caine, chair of the joint chiefs of staff, recently wrote in a letter that the US military had no plans to deploy troops to polling sites during the upcoming November midterm elections.
Caine’s letter came in response to a request for information from senator Elissa Slotkin amid concerns that the Trump administration could send US military personnel to patrol polling sites.

In his letter to Slotkin, Caine said: “The joint force has no plans to send federal military personnel or federalized members of the national guard to polling places during the 2026 elections.” He added that there were “no plans to use such personnel to seize ballots, voting machines, or other election-related material”.

articles.title: Hannah Einbinder, Emma Seligman and others sign letter challenging antisemitism claims against Mark Ruffalo
articles.summary: More than 170 Jewish members of the entertainment industry, including Hannah Einbinder, Ilana Glazer, Joel Coen and Canadian filmmaker Emma Seligman, have signed an open letter defending American…

image.caption: More than 170 Jewish members of the entertainment industry have signed an open letter defending American actor Mark Ruffalo, pictured here in Los Angeles in September 2025, from what it calls an 'outrageous smear campaign.' (Jesse Grant/Getty Images for HBO)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

More than 170 Jewish members of the entertainment industry, including Hannah Einbinder, Ilana Glazer, Joel Coen and Canadian filmmaker Emma Seligman, have signed an open letter defending American actor Mark Ruffalo from what the letter calls an "outrageous smear campaign."
Letter signed by 170 says Ruffalo is facing 'smear campaign' after posts on Skydance-Warner Bros/ merger

More than 170 Jewish members of the entertainment industry, including Hannah Einbinder, Joel Coen and Canadian filmmaker Emma Seligman, have signed an open letter defending American actor Mark Ruffalo from what they called an "outrageous smear campaign."
"We are Jewish artists, writers, creative professionals, faith leaders and thinkers who have ... a simple message to share with the world," reads the letter, published Tuesday. "Enough!"

The letter says Ruffalo has been facing "the false and dangerous weaponization of charges of antisemitism" for speaking out against Paramount Skydance's proposed acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery and drawing connections between the deal and the war in Gaza.

Paramount Skydance is 47 per cent owned by CEO David Ellison and his father, Larry Ellison, who is also co-founder and chief technology officer of Oracle. The Austin-based technology company has been open about its support of Israel, with a top executive previously acknowledging that Oracle shared technology with the Israeli army.
CBC News has reached out to Ruffalo's representatives, as well as Paramount Skydance and Oracle, for comment.

items: Thousands in the film industry pledge to not work with 'complicit' Israeli institutions
Canadian filmmakers, Hollywood celebrities urge TIFF to cut ties with RBC

blocks.text: In a statement to TheWrap and other outlets last month, Paramount said Ruffalo invoked antisemitic tropes when criticizing the deal.

"Words like 'genocide' and 'apartheid,' applied to a corporate transaction, aren't just wrong — they're a bridge too far, and they cheapen the very real suffering those words are meant to describe," the statement said.

An earlier letter signed by more than 1,000 Jewish members of the entertainment industry similarly condemned the actor's statements for "singling out Jewish executives" with "terms lifted from centuries-old antisemitic conspiracy theories."
Ruffalo has not publicly commented on Tuesday's letter, though he has since reshared a video on Instagram criticizing the proposed merger.

He has previously called the accusations of antisemitism against him "appalling and fundamentally dishonest" in a post on X, saying his criticisms were limited to "the actions of the Israeli prime minister, a military technology contract or the executives who supply it."
"My views ... should never be interpreted as hostility toward Jewish people, for whom I have deep love and respect."

The letter released Tuesday is the latest in an ongoing clash between Ruffalo and Paramount. The potential acquisition, valued at $110 billion US, has been delayed until June 2027 after 12 U.S. state attorneys general sued to block it over anti-competition concerns.
A merged Paramount Skydance-Warner would create one of the largest studios in Hollywood, controlling massive properties such as Harry Potter, the DC superhero franchise and CNN.

Other signatories to the latest open letter defending Ruffalo include author Naomi Klein, retired rabbi David Mivasair and physician Gabor Maté, who are all Canadian, as well as American actor Ilana Glazer and filmmaker Jane Schoenbrun.
"We stand proudly with Mark Ruffalo," the letter reads, "and with all decent people who are bravely rising and speaking truth to power."

items: Paramount agrees to delay closing Warner Bros. buyout for months while judge considers states' challenge

blocks.text: 'A classic antitrust case'

On Aug. 21, Ruffalo criticized the merger in a series of Instagram stories, focusing in particular on Oracle for its dealings with the Israeli military. (Ruffalo is an outspoken critic of Israel's military actions in Gaza.)
He reposted a video of Oracle executive vice-chair Safra Catz speaking at the Israeli-American Council National Summit in Washington, D.C., in late 2024.
"There's a few things that we did that I really can't talk about ... to advance the agenda for the Israeli military," said Catz, who was then the company's CEO.
"We have some really profoundly scary technology at Oracle, and we wanted to make sure that it was available for the effort, let's just say that."
A spokesperson for Catz later told the Hollywood Reporter that the technology in question was meant for rescuing hostages taken during the Hamas attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023.
In his Aug. 21 post, Ruffalo said the Palestinian enclave is experiencing a genocide, "built on an apartheid system of oppression powered by Oracle."
"These [technologies] will most likely be merged into one of the largest media conglomerates in the world and one day used on you," he wrote, without going into further detail.

Israel has adamantly and repeatedly denied that its actions in Gaza constitute genocide, calling such accusations "wholly unfounded" and insisting it is targeting militants, not civilians, and aims to safeguard its security.

Ruffalo in his post also called the potential Skydance-Warner merger a "classic antitrust case," saying it would result in a loss of jobs, higher prices for consumers and reduced competition in the industry.

Paramount, which itself was bought by Skydance last year, has previously said the U.S. states' lawsuit pausing the merger "distorts settled antitrust law," maintaining that it would instead create a stronger competitor against other dominant streaming and tech platforms that have harmed the theatrical exhibition market.
Israel rejects Trump's Gaza peace plan
Oracle's support of Israel is well documented. Soon after the Oct. 7 attack, the company posted a message supporting the country, declaring its "solidarity with Israel in the fight against terror."
It also announced a donation of $1 million US to Magen David Adom, the country's national emergency service.

"We knew we might lose customers because of our support for Israel, but it didn't matter to us," said Shmulik Hauzer, who leads sales at Oracle Israel, in an interview with Ynet in 2025. "Supporting Israel is in our DNA — even if it costs us clients. That's our agenda."

The war in Gaza began after that Hamas-led attack on Israel, which by Israeli figures killed around 1,200 people and left 251 taken hostage into Gaza. More than 73,000 people in Gaza have been killed in the war since, according to Palestinian officials.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Hanna Lee is a copy editor at CBC News. You can contact her at hanna.lee@cbc.ca.
With files from Reuters

articles.title: Army secretary resigns after clashes with Hegseth as Democrats warn of ‘hollowed out’ leadership
articles.summary:
The sudden departure of Daniel Driscoll comes after Pentagon chief removed senior officers and blocked promotions, prompting warnings of a leadership crisis

A senior Senate Democrat accused…

blocks.text: A senior Senate Democrat accused Pentagon secretary Pete Hegseth of having “hollowed out” the Army’s senior ranks after its top civilian leader resigned after months of internal clashes with Hegseth.

No official reason was given for army secretary Daniel Driscoll’s departure after 18 months on the job, while thousands of US soldiers are deployed in the Middle East. In a statement on Monday night, White House spokesperson Anna Kelly said Driscoll had been “highly effective in advancing President Trump’s agenda”, citing his work on “readiness and lethality” and his role in Russia-Ukraine negotiations.
Democrats and Republicans alike praised Driscoll’s leadership, but in a statement, Senator Jack Reed, the ranking member on the Senate Armed Services Committee, said he did “not welcome” it.

“It is far past time for President Trump to recognize the lasting harm that Pete Hegseth is inflicting on the Department of Defense,” Reed said. “In the Army alone, he has fired and blocked the promotions of dozens of senior officers without explanation, including Army Chief of Staff General Randy George and half of all four-star generals.
“Secretary Hegseth is cultivating a culture where dissent is punished and competence is secondary to personal allegiance.”

An army official told CBS News that Driscoll spoke with Trump about the “current state” of the army before submitting his resignation. NBC News, citing a source familiar with the matter, reported that in that conversation Driscoll raised concerns about the army’s transformation and readiness and about Hegseth’s blocking those efforts by firing the generals responsible for them.

The public rupture traces back to April, when Hegseth forced out the army’s chief of staff, Gen Randy George, along with two other senior officers. George had worked with Driscoll on the Army Transformation Initiative, an effort to shift the service toward drones and faster weapons acquisition based on lessons from the war in Ukraine. Driscoll later told Congress he considered George “a transformational leader” and said he went to George’s house the day he learned of the firing.

Driscoll sought the help of JD Vance, a friend since law school, as tensions with Hegseth deteriorated, the Washington Post reported. Driscoll also told the Post then that he had no plans to leave his post. “I have no plans to depart or resign as the Secretary of the Army,” he said.

Since George’s departure, the army has moved to scale back a drone unit he and Driscoll had championed, returning it to a conventional infantry role, CBS has reported. Hegseth also removed four Army colonels from consideration for promotion to brigadier general, over objections from Driscoll and George.

Driscoll’s exit adds to a string of senior departures under Hegseth, including navy secretary John Phelan, Southern Command chief Adm Alvin Holsey, and Gen Chris Donahue, who commanded US army forces in Europe and Africa. Sean Parnell, Hegseth’s chief spokesperson, had privately expressed interest in the army secretary post before it became vacant, the Hill has reported, and is among those reportedly under consideration to succeed Driscoll.

“The Pentagon right now is in some cases rudderless, without leadership at the senior rungs of the uniform offices and even in the civilian offices,” Representative Jason Crow, a Democrat and former army ranger who serves on the House Armed Services Committee, told reporters. “I’m gravely concerned about it.”
Driscoll, an Iraq war veteran who worked in finance and technology before joining the administration, also served as a Trump-appointed negotiator in talks to end the Russian war on Ukraine.
Neither the White House nor the Pentagon has said what Driscoll told Trump in their final conversation or how the president responded.

articles.title: Pilandok slightly weakens as habagat prevails over Luzon, Visayas
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Tropical Storm Pilandok slightly decelerated while moving east-northeastward over the Philippine Sea, while the southwest monsoon, or habagat, will continue to prevail over…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Tropical Storm Pilandok slightly decelerated while moving east-northeastward over the Philippine Sea, while the southwest monsoon, or habagat, will continue to prevail over Luzon and Visayas on Wednesday, according to the state weather bureau.

In its 5 a.m. weather forecast, the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (Pagasa) said that weather specialist Chenel Dominguez reported Pilandok was last estimated to be 1,205 kilometers east-northeast of extreme northern Luzon as of 4 a.m.

It slightly decelerated as it moved east-northeastward at 10 kilometers per hour (kph), compared with its previous speed of 15 kph. It maintained its strength, with maximum sustained winds of 65 kph and gustiness of up to 80 kph.

Dominguez maintained Pagasa’s earlier forecast that Pilandok will not directly affect the country as it continues to be far from our landmass. Meanwhile, she said that the habagat will bring concentrated rains over the western section of the country.
She added that while Metro Manila and nearby areas may experience fair weather conditions, isolated rainshowers and localized thunderstorms are still possible in the afternoon and evening.
Hot and humid conditions with chances of localized thunderstorms are expected over Visayas and Mindanao.
She also shared that the habagat will bring strong to gale-force gusts over these areas:

items: From Wednesday until Thursday (September 3): Most of Luzon and Visayas, Zamboanga del Norte, Misamis Occidental, Lanao del Norte, Misamis Oriental, Camiguin, Dinagat Islands, Davao Occidental, and Davao Oriental

blocks.text: Weather disturbances outside the PAR
Meanwhile, Dominguez shared that two weather disturbances are being monitored outside the Philippine area of responsibility (PAR).

Tropical Storm Saudel, formerly called Obet, was last located 560 kilometers west of Itbayat, Batanes. Dominguez said that it currently has no direct effect in the country and has a low chance of re-entering the PAR.
On the other hand, the low pressure area spotted 2,935 kilometers east of Central Luzon is unlikely to develop into a tropical depression. /jpv

articles.title: US may require parents to prove citizenship to get passports for their children
articles.summary:
Proposal is how state department could enforce Trump’s executive order targeting what it calls ‘birth tourism’

The US state department has proposed requiring parents applying for passports…

blocks.text: The US state department has proposed requiring parents applying for passports for their children to provide proof of their own citizenship or immigration status as part of Donald Trump’s ⁠latest effort to limit birthright citizenship.

The ⁠draft guidance, reviewed by ​Reuters, is the first detailed look at how the state department could enforce Trump’s 6 August executive order targeting what it calls “birth tourism” and broadening historical exceptions to birthright citizenship.

The White House referred Reuters questions to the state department. ⁠In a statement, state department spokesman Tommy Pigott said: “President Trump has been unequivocal that this administration will protect the meaning and value of American citizenship, full stop, and that includes making sure our passport adjudication process fully reflects that standard.”

Limiting birthright ⁠citizenship has been one of the president’s top priorities in his far-reaching crackdown on immigration. The US supreme court ruled his previous attempt violated the country’s constitution.

Trump’s initial ​executive order would have granted automatic US citizenship at birth only to ‌children with at least one parent who ‌was a US citizen or a lawful permanent resident known as a green card holder.
In a 6-3 ruling, the supreme court found the order was unlawful, ‌with a majority finding it violated the citizenship clause of the US constitution’s 14th amendment.

Trump’s August 6 order was narrower, taking particular aim at “birth tourism” in which women travel to the United States to give birth so their children can obtain automatic citizenship. That order could still be blocked in court.

The new directive would withhold citizenship from children with a parent who works for a foreign government in the US, is engaged in fraud or a commercial transaction to obtain citizenship, or is classified as an “alien enemy”.

“The department will require parental information and evidence of parental citizenship or immigration status ‌as part of its determination whether the applicant is subject to EO 14418,” the state department draft guidance reads, citing the executive order number.

If implemented, the proposal would require all parents or legal guardians to provide proof of their citizenship, such as ​a valid US passport or birth certificate, or evidence of their immigration status, such as an I-94 form or a legal permanent residency card, when submitting a passport application for their children. The information would be used by the government to determine if the child qualifies for citizenship under the new order, the state department proposal says.

Currently, parents whose children were born in the US only need to prove their parentage and present photo identification during this process. They are also asked to check a ⁠box on the application form indicating if they are US citizens but are not required to file supporting documentation.

Lawyers ​pursuing class-action lawsuits on behalf of babies who would be ​deprived of citizenship under Trump’s initial order have asked ​two different federal judges to prevent his latest order from taking effect.

articles.title: Two sides in Alberta separation debate entrenched, with majority wanting to remain in Canada: poll
articles.summary: With fewer than 50 days until this October’s referendum, a new poll suggests Albertans remain entrenched in long-held positions tied to the idea of separating from Canada.

image.caption: Alberta Premier Danielle Smith, left, waits to deliver a speech on Alberta Day in Calgary on Aug. 30. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Calgary·New
With fewer than 50 days until this October’s referendum, a new poll suggests Albertans remain entrenched in long-held positions tied to the idea of separating from Canada.
Majority of respondents in favour of immigration reforms in October’s referendum, Research Co. poll says

The Research Co. poll from August found 74 per cent of respondents would vote for Alberta to remain in Canada, while 22 per cent would vote for the Government of Alberta to start the legal process required to hold a second, binding referendum on leaving the country.

Support for the idea of a binding referendum was highest among Albertans aged 35 to 54, at 27 per cent. Twenty per cent of Albertans aged 55 and older voiced support for a further referendum, while 18 per cent of those aged 18 to 34 agreed with the idea.
Public opinion polls, including for CBC News, have consistently shown a majority of Albertans support staying in Canada.
“Even though we still have a few weeks left to go in this campaign, people seem to be very set in their ways,” Mario Canseco, president of the Vancouver-based polling firm, told CBC News.
“This is definitely not a situation that has winning conditions for the side that wants to separate.”

The results come from an online survey of 750 likely voters in Alberta, conducted by Research Co. between Aug. 24 and 26. The survey has a margin of error of +/- 3.6 percentage points, 19 times out of 20.

Canseco asks the question around separation about once per year, tracing back to Rachel Notley’s time as Alberta premier. Numbers typically range around 25 to 30 per cent who say they like the idea of secession, he said.

Those numbers track with other polling. In April, a poll directed by Janet Brown Opinion Research for CBC News found 27 per cent said they’d vote for separation, while 67 per cent said they’d vote against it.

items: Support for Alberta separatism flat, struggling high earners more likely supporters: poll
Majority of Albertans would vote to stay in Canada, find Smith's handling poor: poll

blocks.text: With time ticking toward the Oct. 19 referendum vote, federalist and separatist groups have been ramping up their voter mobilization efforts.
But pollsters like Canseco have found there are few who don’t have their minds made up.

“There’s a tiny level of undecideds when we ask about the separation question — only four per cent,” Canseco said of his latest poll’s findings. “Usually, when you have an election or a referendum, the level of undecideds is higher — maybe 10 to 15 per cent.”
Differences on immigration, constitutional reform
Though Research Co. found the idea of holding a binding vote on separation is “not resonating with the public,” the same can’t uniformly be said when it comes to the other ballots.
In addition to the separation question, October’s referendum includes five questions tied to immigration and four to constitutional reform.

items: Follow all of our Alberta referendum coverage

blocks.text: Ranging from 58 to 66 per cent, a majority of likely voters said they would vote “yes” on the five questions related to immigration, according to the poll.

“This is an issue that the government has really connected well on, because you do have people who maybe voted for the NDP in the last election of Alberta, who voted for the Liberals in the last election in Canada, who look at this as an interesting idea,” Canseco said.
The most popular of the proposals is the ballot question asking about requiring proof of citizenship when voting, with 66 per cent support.

On the lower end, 58 per cent said they’d be in favour of a law mandating only Canadian citizens, permanent residents and individuals with an “Alberta-approved” immigration status would be eligible for provincially-funded programs like health care and education.

items: Immigration is on the ballot. Here’s what some of Alberta’s multicultural communities say about the referendum
What some immigrants could lose if Alberta votes yes to Danielle Smith's questions

blocks.text: The federalist group Alberta's Voice, run by political strategist Stephen Carter, is behind the “no to the nine” signs, encouraging voters to reject the ballot questions.
Carter said he believes people are starting to ask themselves what the nine other questions actually mean, and that will lead to a decline in support leading up to referendum day.
He doesn’t think most Albertans want the government to implement the kinds of policies he believes the questions will lead to.
“I think that as people become more aware of what these actual questions are asking, we’ll see the numbers start to drop,” he said.
“But for now, it’s fairly easy just to say yes to these questions, even while saying no to leaving Canada.”
The Research Co. poll found that public support was lower on the four questions tied to constitutional reform, ranging from 39 to 46 per cent support.

items: Albertans to vote on judicial appointments as premier argues ‘distinct legal traditions’
Once seeking Senate reform, Alberta now ponders voting to be ‘rid of the darn thing’

blocks.text: Tanya Clemens, co-leader of the Alberta independence group Let Alberta Decide, said the higher support for the questions on constitutional reforms — compared to the separation question — shows a gap in understanding what a vote for independence promises to deliver.

“It was close to a majority wanting constitutional changes. I don’t know if they understand that by voting [to remain], it’s basically voting for status quo and for things to stay the same,” Clemens said.
“It doesn’t give Alberta any more leverage. So to me, it looks like there’s some more education that needs to happen.”
The poll also found that likely voters in Alberta thought the validity of the referendum as a “true representation of the wishes of the public” depends on voter turnout.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Joel is a reporter/editor with CBC Calgary. In fall 2021, he spent time with CBC's bureau in Lethbridge. He was previously the editor of the Airdrie City View and Rocky View Weekly newspapers. He hails from Swift Current, Sask. Reach him by email at joel.dryden@cbc.ca
