articles.title: DA, NIA ask for more funding in 2027 as response to El Niño effects
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Agriculture (DA) and National Irrigation Administration (NIA) on Tuesday appealed for budget increases in some of their projects to respond to the possible…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Agriculture (DA) and National Irrigation Administration (NIA) on Tuesday appealed for budget increases in some of their projects to respond to the possible impacts of El Niño in the country.

During the House committee on appropriations’ briefing on the budget proposal of the two agencies, committee chairperson Rep. Mikaela Suansing asked both agencies if they allotted contingency funds under the 2027 National Expenditure Program for possible effects of El Niño on farmers and fisherfolk.

Agriculture Secretary Francisco Tiu Laurel Jr. said that his agency needs budget increases for the Presidential Assistance for Farmers and Fisherfolk (PAF), noting that the distribution rate of PAF for this year stood at 57.67 percent and may be exhausted by next month due to the effects of southwest monsoon to the livelihoods of farmers and fisherfolk.

He added that the agency needs another P8.7 billion for the fertilizer assistance funds for farmers and additional P10 billion to P12 billion for fisherfolk under the programs of the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources.

Meanwhile, NIA Administrator Eduardo Guillen asked the House lawmakers for an increase in the agency’s quick response fund (QRF). He shared that the NIA only has P300 million allotted for its QRF this year, which he said will not be enough.
Suansing then asked them to categorize the items allotted for El Niño response, noting that this is for them to give special consideration to their requests.

The Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration earlier said that a moderate to strong El Niño is present in the Tropical Pacific. Citing climate models, it added that El Niño will persist until the first half of 2027 and may reach a very strong state until the end of 2026. /cb

articles.title: War and sanctions deepen Iran's fuel crisis
articles.summary: Long lines at fuel stations are spreading across Iran as war damage, import constraints and new US sanctions squeeze supplies.

image.caption: In cities across Iran, drivers are reporting hours-long waits at filling stationsImage: Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Only days after Washington announced a new round of economic sanctions on Iran, the country's gasoline shortage has become increasingly visible on the streets.

In cities across Iran, drivers are reporting hours-long waits at filling stations. Videos circulating on social media show some people arriving before midnight or sleeping in their cars to secure fuel the following morning. Some stations have closed before serving everyone in line.

The situation is even more difficult for diesel. Truck drivers say queues at filling stations near major cities can stretch for kilometers, forcing them to wait overnight simply to obtain enough fuel to return to work.

Iran already faces a gasoline deficit of roughly 15 million liters a day. War damage, difficulties importing refined products and a tightening US blockade have made an old structural problem much harder to manage.
Is Iran set to become an economic outcast?
Hours in line for a few liters
A resident of Karaj, west of Tehran, told DW that some filling stations were limiting individual purchases to around five liters.

"I'm in the gasoline line right now. It took about 45 minutes just to get this far," he said. "Yesterday I went to several stations. Some were closed, some had no gasoline and others had very long queues."
He said he returned at 6 a.m. the next morning hoping to avoid the crowds but again found a long line.
He suspects the shortages are partly being used to prepare public opinion for higher gasoline prices, a claim that cannot be independently verified.
For truck drivers, waiting means losing income.

"Our whole life is either spent in the diesel line or on the road," one driver said. He described sleeping at a station while waiting for a tanker that might arrive around midday and supply only a few dozen trucks.
Another driver said he had been waiting since 8 a.m. after failing to obtain diesel the previous day.
For drivers whose earnings depend directly on keeping their vehicles moving, every lost day adds to rising insurance, tire, oil, repair and maintenance costs.
Is Iran changing its gasoline?
The shortage has coincided with the use of methanol in domestically produced gasoline.
Vahid Ghaneifard, chief executive of Persian Gulf Star Oil Company, recently confirmed that the refinery had begun testing methanol as an oxygenate in its gasoline.
The company says methanol makes up around 0.5% of the mixture. Iran's refining authorities say the national fuel standard permits methanol concentrations of up to 3%.
Officials insist the trial complies with technical requirements.
But the timing has fueled public suspicion.
Videos shared online show motorists holding bottles of unusually clear fuel and claiming that gasoline quality has deteriorated.
Why Iran fuel crisis hits different in Europe than the US
Some have alleged that water or excessive alcohol is being mixed into supplies. The allegations have not been independently corroborated.

There has, however, been at least one confirmed incident involving water contamination. In Rafsanjan, local authorities acknowledged that water had mixed with gasoline at a filling station after videos showed cars and motorcycles experiencing problems following refueling.
Officials said the incident resulted from a technical fault and was being investigated.
Distrust over fuel quality grows
For motorists already facing shortages, isolated incidents can reinforce wider fears.

A Tehran resident told DW he had spent about 1 billion tomans — roughly $5,250 (€4,529) at current exchange rates — repairing his car after its crankshaft failed. He believes poor-quality gasoline caused the damage, though such a connection has not been independently established.
He said he was reluctant to publicly protest.
Another resident in Rey, south of Tehran, told DW that motorists had gathered outside a filling station after several cars were allegedly damaged following refueling.
The concern is not simply technical, as it reflects a deeper collapse of trust between consumers and authorities at a time when the government is also discussing higher gasoline and diesel prices.
Tehran argues that the current subsidy system encourages excessive consumption and smuggling and imposes an unsustainable burden on state finances.
But consumers point to other issues such as inefficient cars, inadequate public transport and incomes that have failed to keep pace with inflation.
Can new US sanctions cut off Iran's oil revenue?
Is a price increase in the works?
Economist Hassan Mansour believes the government is once again preparing the political ground for higher energy prices.

Officials have repeatedly argued that Iranian gasoline prices are artificially low, that large volumes are smuggled abroad and that the economy consumes far more energy per unit of output than comparable countries.
The proposed solution is to bring domestic fuel prices closer to international levels.
"Once again, the government finds itself preparing the ground for raising the price of energy carriers," Mansour told DW.
But the problem runs deeper than subsidized gasoline.

Mansour points to the financial condition of Iran's oil industry. Budget documents indicate that the National Iranian Oil Company has tens of billions of euros in debt to the central bank and commercial banks, while the company also owes substantial sums to the National Development Fund and faces major tax liabilities.
When these debts cannot realistically be repaid, Mansour argues, they weaken state finances and contribute indirectly to currency instability and inflation.
Raising gasoline prices could therefore serve both as a demand-management measure and a source of additional revenue.
How the Iran war has deepened Saudi-UAE rivalry
A politically dangerous choice
The government has few easy options.
While imports are harder to finance and transport, domestic production is struggling to keep pace with consumption.
Increasing output quickly requires investment and technology, while reducing consumption means either rationing fuel more aggressively or raising prices. Yet both carry political risks.
Iranian authorities remember what happened in November 2019, when a sudden gasoline price increase triggered nationwide protests followed by a deadly crackdown and an internet shutdown.
Today the economic environment is considerably more fragile.
War has damaged infrastructure, international sanctions are tightening and household purchasing power has fallen sharply. Long fuel queues are now adding another source of frustration.
For Tehran, raising prices might help reduce the gasoline deficit.
But doing so while people are already waiting overnight for fuel could turn an energy shortage into another crisis of public anger, which is something far more difficult to control.

articles.title: Robin Padilla says trip via NLEX to San Simon took 7 hours, Lito Lapid misses impeachment trial
articles.summary: Senators were among those who experienced the horrendous traffic jam on both lanes of the North Luzon Expressway caused by flooding in the San Simon area.

blocks.text: Senators were among those who experienced the horrendous traffic jam on both lanes of the North Luzon Expressway caused by flooding in the San Simon area.
According to Mark Salazar's report on "24 Oras," Sen. Robin Padilla told the Senate plenary about his seven-hour trip from his home to San Simon in Pampanga.
Sen. Joel Villanueva, on the other hand, narrated how Sen. Lito Lapid missed the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte because of the congestion on the expressway.
Padilla shared the long hours they spent queuing on NLEX and presented a video documenting his ordeal from Monday.

“Umalis po kami ng 4:30 ng umaga galing po sa aming bat cave, sa tahanan… Nakalabas po kami ng San Simon 11:30 na ng tanghali. Pitong oras po… sa San Simon lang po 'yon, hindi pa kami nakarating ng Pangasinan,“ Padilla shared.
(We left at 4:30 in the morning from our home… We only managed to exit San Simon at 11:30 in the morning. That was seven hours… just in San Simon alone, and we hadn’t even reached Pangasinan yet.)

“Hindi din po passable doon, 95% ng mga lugar ng San Simon ay lubog. Pagbalik po namin ng NLEX, iniisip namin baka bumaba na ‘yung tubig. Makikita niyo po sa video mas tumaas pa 'yung tubig,” he added.
(It was impassable there; 95% of San Simon was submerged. When we returned to NLEX, we thought the water might have receded. But as you can see in the video, the floodwaters rose even higher.)
Padilla called the experience on the expressway unfair, emphasizing that motorists pay tolls to use it.

“Nagbayad ka naman. [Sana] una na lang sinabi na nila na hindi ganon ang mararanasan namin dahil expressway nga eh. Pero ganon pa man po, wala din naman talagang dadaanan dahil doon po sa McArthur Highway ay lubog din,” Padilla said.

(You paid for it. They should have warned us that this is what we would experience on an expressway. But even then, there was really no alternative route because MacArthur Highway was also submerged.)
Villanueva said Lapid's ordeal at the San Simon segment of NLEX prevented him from attending the earlier impeachment trial.
“Reports showed the traffic stretching as far as 10 km, Mr. President, 10 kilometro po. Some motorists reported spending up to 22 hours,” Villanueva said.

“Gusto natin malaman, Mr. President, at itanong sa NLEX Corporation, nabigyan ba agad ng tulong ang ating mga kababayan nating na-stranded? May tubig po ba, may pagkain [o] portalets at medical assistance po ba?” he added.
(We want to know, Mr. President, and ask NLEX Corporation: Was immediate assistance provided to our stranded motorists? Was there water, food, portable toilets, or medical assistance?)
Villanueva similarly pointed out the toll motorists pay to traverse NLEX, urging expressway management to consider waiving fees or offering refunds to those trapped in the traffic.

“Ang NLEX po, hindi libre ang pagpasok ho diyan. Dapat ikonsidera ng NLEX management ang pag-waive o pag-refund ng toll fees para sa mga motoristang matinding naapektuhan. Nagbabayad ka ng toll, naiipit ka pa sa baha,” the senator said.
(Entering NLEX is not free, so NLEX management should consider waiving or refunding toll fees for severely affected motorists. You pay a toll, only to get trapped in a flood.)
He also stressed that traffic advisories regarding conditions on NLEX must be issued promptly, and that sufficient personnel should be deployed to assist stranded motorists.

The senators’ discussion of the NLEX traffic ordeal led to broader concerns regarding anomalous flood mitigation projects across the country, as well as the status of a previously proposed flood control master plan.

Senator Vicente “Tito” Sotto III noted that a comprehensive master plan had been developed under the leadership of former Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) Secretary Rogelio "Babes" Singson.

“Secretary Babes Singson of the Department of Public Works created and formulated a flood control [plan] from north to south. They started the study sometime in 2011, and by 2015 it… became a master plan and they were about to execute,” Sotto said.
“Unfortunately, there were elections in 2016 and the program, I believe, was sidelined,” he added.
Padilla questioned which agency would be entrusted to craft such a master plan moving forward.

“Napakaganda po ng mungkahi ng ating idolo rin, dati pong Senate President Vicente Sotto. ‘Yun pong masterplan, ang tanong ko lang po, sino po bang gagawa na naman niyan? DPWH po ba ang gagawa? Medyo di po ba tayo napapaso na ba?” Padilla said.

(The suggestion of former Senate President Vicente Sotto is very good. My only question regarding that master plan is: who will draft it this time? Will it be the DPWH again? Haven't we been burned enough?)
For her part, Senator Risa Hontiveros brought up the proposed mega-dike project that local government units in Pampanga have long been requesting.

“Fino-follow up ng mga barangay captain noon mula sa Pampanga ay ‘yun daw meg adike na matagal nang ipinapanukala, panahon pa yata ni dating Pangulong Macapagal Arroyo. Ano na po ba ang nangyari doon?” Hontiveros said.

(What the barangay captains from Pampanga were following up on back then was the mega-dike project that has been proposed for a long time, back during the administration of former President Macapagal-Arroyo. What ever happened to that?) –Jean Mangaluz/NB, GMA News

articles.title: Norway's Haakon takes oath as mourners pay respects to late King
articles.summary: Norway's new King takes the first major step of his reign as his father, the late King Harald V, lies in state at the Royal Palace.

blocks.text: Norway's Haakon VIII has sworn an oath before parliament in Oslo in the first major step of his reign as King.
During Tuesday's ceremony, parliament also held a minute's silence for Haakon's father, the late King Harald V, who died on Friday.
Haakon's wife, Queen Mette-Marit, was absent from the formalities as she continues to recover from a lung transplant.
Following the ceremony, mourners began paying their respects at the late King's coffin, which is lying in state at the Royal Palace until 8 September.

articles.title: Rice imports may hit 5M tons amid drought, monsoon risks – DA
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines – The Philippines may need to import as much as five million metric tons of rice to secure stocks as storms, monsoon rains, and a developing El Niño drought threaten the harvest,…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – The Philippines may need to import as much as five million metric tons of rice to secure stocks as storms, monsoon rains, and a developing El Niño drought threaten the harvest, Agriculture Secretary Francisco Tiu Laurel Jr. said on Tuesday.

At a congressional briefing on the 2027 budget, Tiu Laurel said the government is looking to shore up rice stocks to withstand severe weather, with imports eyed to cover next year’s first-quarter consumption.
“It’s better that we are prepared with enough supply rather than fall short,” he told lawmakers in Filipino.

About four million metric tons of rice have been imported so far, and shipments would likely taper during the wet harvest season before ramping up again afterward, Tiu Laurel said. The country’s rice production target this year was pegged at 19 million metric tons, he added.
“Towards the end of this year, after our harvest season, we have to carry out additional importation… so that we are ready for the first quarter of next year,” he said.
“We are already front-loading what we need for the first quarter of 2027. And we need to maintain more than a 60-day buffer because the climate is different now,” he added.
The Philippines is the world’s top rice buyer, and monsoon rains alongside a looming record El Niño could trigger a drought that could squeeze supplies of the staple grain and drive up food prices.
Last year, the country imported 3.39 million metric tons.
‘Precautionary’
Tiu Laurel said the record importation is merely a preemptive move to secure supplies after being asked what his agency is doing to boost domestic output.
“What we are doing this year is all precautionary,” he said.
He said the government’s thrust remains prioritizing local production and boosting yields, noting that the average output per hectare of farmland “is increasing.”
“Our average yield per hectare is rising. It’s just that we’re really being hit by disasters like typhoons, flooding, and now El Niño,” Tiu Laurel said.
The Department of Agriculture is continuing its mechanization efforts to make harvesting more efficient, including putting up 380 drying equipment nationwide for unhusked rice and corn, he said.
Expanding irrigation coverage is also a priority for the government, alongside research on inbred and hybrid seeds to develop resilient rice varieties, he added.

“We also have a new policy to push: if you want to import, you’ll be required to invest in the local industry, in its infrastructure, and you’ll need to buy palay from our farmers in order to secure an import allocation,” Tiu Laurel said. /mcm

articles.title: MapQuest app reaches No 1 on US Apple list after defying Trump’s Lake Ontario order
articles.summary:
Navigating app surpasses Google and Apple Maps on top-downloaded US chart after posting ‘we’re not changing it’

A pioneering online mapping app that defied

blocks.text: A pioneering online mapping app that defied Donald Trump by refusing to rename Lake Ontario has become the most in-demand navigation tool in the US.

MapQuest, which was openly dismissive of the president’s 27 August executive order directing federal agencies to refer to the smallest of the Great Lakes as “Lake America” amid a trade spat with Canada, leapfrogged rivals Google Maps and Apple Maps to top the most-downloaded list, as first reported by TechCrunch.
The app held the No 1 spot on Apple’s App Store as of Tuesday morning, the Guardian confirmed.
Google quickly capitulated to Trump’s demand, showing Lake America to US customers, while Apple is reportedly mulling a decision under pressure from the White House to make the same change.
But MapQuest, a 30-year-old company that bills itself as “the OG” (original) of the internet mapping era, appears to have been rewarded for standing firm.

TechCrunch said the app’s downloads had “soared” in recent days to become the fourth most popular of all apps in the US, excluding games – and to lead the Apple app store’s navigation chart, with Google at No 2.
In Canada, meanwhile, MapQuest was the second-most downloaded app overall by Sunday night.

It comes as polls show Trump’s efforts at renaming the lake found favor with only 14% of Americans, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll published on Tuesday. And that survey found only slightly more, 20%, approved of higher tariffs imposed by the Trump administration on Canadian goods, with 57% opposed.

MapQuest’s general manager, Doug Berger, said in a statement that usage of its app was running at about 50 times its usual rate. As a bit of fun, he said, the company was also offering subscribers the chance to generate their own name for the lake.

That was courtesy of a tool it first introduced after Trump rebranded the Gulf of Mexico to the “Gulf of America” among US federal government agencies in 2025 – to which Google also acquiesced in the American market.
Berger said in a statement: “We took the same approach we did with the Gulf of Mexico: be part of the conversation, and give people an app that keeps the names they’re familiar with.
“Hundreds of thousands of people signaled to us this weekend that we got it right, by downloading our app.”
MapQuest has maintained its defiance, and some might say mockery, of Trump’s Lake Ontario order since an original “We’re not changing it” post on social media on 27 August.

The following day, in an all-capital letter post similar in style and language to those favored by the president, it wrote: “Our maps are big and beautiful. People come up to us and say we’ll get them places. And we do!”

It also responded to a poster who expressed surprise that MapQuest still existed and was not “in the same grave” as RadioShack, the once prominent US technology and electronics company that went through two bankruptcies and shuttered its retail locations a decade ago.
“Understandable but the other OG, @RadioShackUSA, is still here too,” MapQuest replied, noting its continued existence as an e-commerce operation.

On Tuesday morning, Apple Maps continued to show the body of water spanning the US-Canada border as Lake Ontario, despite the insistence on Monday of Doug Burgum, Trump’s interior secretary, that he was “confident” it would soon show Lake America after the president contacted the company directly.
On Google, its map for US users reflects the change – but remains Lake Ontario, a name it has had for about 400 years, for users in the rest of the world.

Elsewhere, protests continue to escalate. A giant “Lake Ontario – Now and Always” sign in English and French was erected over the weekend near Grimsby, Ontario. Ontario’s premier, Doug Ford, told ABC News: “No one’s going to call it Lake of America. It’s been Lake Ontario for hundreds of years. It’s going to continue being Lake Ontario.”

On Monday, three Democratic US representatives, Tim Kennedy and Joe Morelle of New York, and Debbie Dingell of Michigan, introduced legislation called the Hands Off Our Great Lakes act, seeking to block the Republican president’s federal order to rename the lake, and prevent future changes.

articles.title: Lost island in northern B.C. lake — that appeared and disappeared — located, B.C. Hydro says

image.caption: A photo of this floating island of trees in the Williston Lake reservoir in northern B.C. was taken by a local boater and shared with resident Rocky Avery, who posted it to social media. (Submitted by Rocky Avery)

blocks.text: British Columbia
B.C. Hydro says mini forest bigger than a Canadian football field landed ashore in the Williston Reservoir after drifting some 30 kilometres northwest of its last known location.
Newly formed island found along shore of Williston Reservoir after drifting for 30 kilometres
A newly formed island in B.C.'s largest lake has been located.

B.C. Hydro said Monday that the forested land mass, bigger than a Canadian football field, landed ashore after drifting some 30 kilometres northwest of its last known location in the middle of Williston Reservoir.

The island's curious appearance, and seemingly sudden disappearance in the massive man-made lake in northern B.C., has captured international attention and intrigue since boaters first made the discovery in August.
B.C. Hydro spokesperson Bob Gammer said satellite imagery dated Aug. 15 shows the island resting in the north entrance of the Ospika Arm, where the Ospika River flows into the reservoir.
He said the island appears to be intact, and that it has moved even further away from the W.A.C. Bennett Dam connected to the reservoir.
"For it to disappear and now to reappear, that just creates a lot of excitement," Gammer said.
"It's great to know that we found it and it's not causing any trouble right now and hopefully that's the way it stays."

items: An island mysteriously appeared — then disappeared — on B.C.'s largest reservoir

blocks.text: The island's origin still hasn't been confirmed though B.C. Hydro believes record high water levels likely caused it to break off somewhere along the reservoir's sprawling shoreline.
Gammer said strong winds would have moved it through the open waters over the last month.
"It's certainly not current. The water does very slowly move to the east to the [dam]," Gammer said. "The wind is really what's going to drive things."
Island in Canada mysteriously appears, then vanishes
The Williston reservoir was created in 1968 and is the seventh-largest in the world.
John Clague, an earth sciences professor at Simon Fraser University, said decades of erosion have left the banks of the reservoir vulnerable to landslides.
He said the reservoir is "notorious" for having strong winds that can create waves and currents that undermine shallow rooted trees along the shoreline.
B.C. Hydro estimates the island to be around 70 metres wide and 140 metres long, or about 9,800 square metres in area.
"This has to be a world's record in terms of size for floating wood mats with trees that were quite healthy and growing nicely and now are part of an island," said Clague.
B.C. Hydro will want to get a better understanding of where it came from and how it formed, Clague said.
"There should be a big scar along the shoreline."
Clague said he's surprised how far the island has travelled, and B.C. Hydro will want to investigate to understand where it came from and how it formed.

That's quite a distance for it to travel and not essentially fall apart," he said. "It's a big piece of real estate, but it's thin. It's not like an iceberg that extends further beneath the water in an ocean."
The island's whereabouts have been a curiosity for residents in northern B.C. as well as interested observers from around the world.
Video of the island bobbing in the middle of the reservoir first went viral in local Facebook groups in early August.
After a decade spent running fishing charters on Williston Lake, Marianne Anderson said she has never seen anything like it.
She said a local fishing guide showed her the video of what looked like a giant carpet of trees, bobbing in the middle of the lake.
The next time fishing guides were in the area, the island was gone.
"It looked unreal," she said.
LISTEN | An island mysteriously appeared — then disappeared — in northern B.C.:
Radio West3:57A floating island in northern B.C.'s Williston Reservoir

Finlay Farquhar, a radio engineering assistant based in the United Kingdom, said he was able to track the island's new location using open-source satellite websites after reading about it on social media.
He also found it nestled on the shoreline in the Ospika Arm.
"Quite curious, and it was really quite surprising that there'd been a floating island," Farquhar said. "I was quite surprised by how far it moved."
Gammer said B.C. Hydro was able to locate the island after independently confirming new reports of its location.
Gammer said it's possible the island might move again if strong winds break it free from shore.
"It's nothing that's going to require us to take some serious action," he said.
"We will monitor this just to see what happens, whether it breaks apart and if we then have a debris field instead of one big chunk, that may cause us to take some other action."
He said the island is unstable and boaters should be cautious.

"Go ahead, boat up to it, get near it, take your own pictures, get your drone out, whatever you'd like to do to image it," he said. "But we really warn people about trying to climb on it, as tempting as it may be."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Matt Preprost is a reporter with CBC British Columbia based in Fort St. John. He has covered the B.C Peace region and Northern Rockies since 2013. Email him at fsj@cbc.ca
Katie DeRosa

articles.title: Ex-president Duterte requests ICC chamber to require resubmission of charges
articles.summary: Former President Rodrigo Duterte"s defense team has requested the International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber III to direct the Prosecution to resubmit the document containing the charges (DCC)…

blocks.text: Former President Rodrigo Duterte’s defense team has requested the International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber III to direct the Prosecution to resubmit the document containing the charges (DCC) for allegedly violating Duterte’s right.
In an 11-page document dated August 31, Duterte’s team argued that the DCC violates the former official’s right to be informed in detail of the nature, cause, and content of the charges against him.

Due to this, it appealed to the chamber to order the Prosecution to refile a document that frames the charges “in terms of counts with a defined scope, being crimes under the ICC Statute, and with an exhaustive list of underpinning acts.”
“The accused cannot even begin to make strategic decisions about how to approach this case, because he does not know what case he has to meet,” it said.

“The Duterte charges are a literal moving target; a non-exhaustive, illustrative list of events whose proof beyond reasonable doubt may or may not trigger liability for thousands of others, and whose evidential value remains entirely unclear,” it added.
In April, the ICC confirmed the charges against Duterte cover 49 incidents, which are divided into the following three counts:

Count 1: Murder as a crime against humanity in Davao City during the mayoral period of at least 19 victims, between 2013 and around June 2016, through indirect co-perpetration, ordering and/or inducing, and/or aiding and abetting;

Count 2: Murder as a crime against humanity of ‘high-value targets’ in locations across the Philippines during the presidential period of at least the 14 victims between around July 2016 and July 2017, through indirect co-perpetration, and/or ordering and/or inducing and/or 25(3)(c) (aiding and abetting); and

Count 3: Murder and attempted murder as crimes against humanity in barangay clearance operations in locations across the Philippines during the presidential period of at least the 45 victims (43 murders and two attempted murders) between around July 2016 and September 2018, through indirect co-perpetration, ordering and/or inducing, and/or aiding and abetting.
Duterte’s team noted that it received a notice of details of eight additional incidents submitted by the Prosecution, bringing the total list of incidents to 57.
“[C]onsistent practice has been for charging documents to be divided into topical headings, usually geographical areas with corresponding time periods, or overarching events,” it said.

“Under each topical heading, the counts are then listed together with the legal and factual basis being alleged in support of each. In this way, the accused is duly notified of the allegations in detail, as required,” it added.
According to his defense team, the framing of the DCC is “entirely different and entirely novel.”
“The topical headings have been elevated to the status of counts allegedly committed over an extended period and across a large geographical area,” it said.

The defense team said that a “count” has only ever denoted an individual crime under the ICC Statute. Meanwhile, it said the specific charged acts were relegated to the “status of non-exhaustive and illustrative-only incidents without legal characterization.”
“The Prosecution’s decision to frame the charges in this entirely novel way makes it impossible for the defendant to know what case he has to meet at trial,” it said.
The defense said that it would need to be ready to defend against any unlawful killing over a seven-year-plus period.

“Keeping in mind that the Prosecution had disclosed around 5,000 documents as at the date of the confirmation decision, which has now increased by over 400% to over 25,000 items at the date of writing, the Defence team has no chance of even reading this full volume of disclosure before the start of the trial, let alone being aware of every alleged murder or killing contained therein and being ready to defend against them,” it said.
Aside from this, the defense team said the current charges put the Trial Chamber in an impossible position.

It said that the Chamber must examine whether the act is part of the widespread or systematic attack, considered as a whole with due regard to the nature of the act at issue, its aims and consequences and knowledge of that nexus by the perpetrator of the act.

“Where there are no pleaded underlying acts, but rather only ‘non-exhaustive’ and ‘illustrative’ examples of alleged conduct by perpetrators, the Prosecution can circumvent these requirements,” it said.

“Meaning, that the trial could end with the Prosecution having done nothing more than establishing a certain number of ‘illustrative incidents’ but without any of the requisite contextual elements necessary to link the charged acts back to the charged counts,” it added. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Ford government to begin ripping out, reconfiguring Toronto bike lanes following court of appeal ruling
articles.summary: The Ford government is going ahead with bike lane removal and reconfiguration on some of Toronto's busiest roads, the province announced Tuesday.

blocks.text: Toronto
The Ford government is going ahead with bike lane removal and reconfiguration on some of Toronto's busiest roads, the province announced Tuesday.
Vehicle lanes on sections of Bloor Street W. to be 'immediately' restored, province says
Ford government to begin Toronto bike lane removal. Here's what you need to know

Tuesday's news release says that the provincial government is going to begin the process of "restoring motor vehicle lanes" that were previously removed to make bike lanes on Bloor Street, Yonge Street, University Avenue, Queen's Park, Queen's Park Crescent and Avenue Road.

The release says the province has also issued a request for proposals to "study and provide design options" for restoring vehicle lanes along some "sections" of Toronto's busiest streets. These proposals would look into options for retaining or reconfiguring bike lanes, according to the release.

items: Ontario Court of Appeal says Ford can rip out Toronto bike lanes
Ontario aware bike lane removals may not reduce congestion, could make people less safe: internal documents

blocks.text: "The province is also immediately beginning to restore motor vehicle lanes on Bloor Street W., starting east of a 600-metre section at Clissold Road where vehicle lanes were restored in December 2025," the news release said.

The announcement comes after Ontario's court of appeal ruled in August that the Ford government can rip out 19 kilometres of protected bike lanes in Toronto, reversing a lower-court decision made in July 2025.
Restoring vehicle lanes stops congestion, transport minister says

When asked about bike lane removals at an unrelated news conference Tuesday, Ontario Transportation Minister Prabmeet Sarkaria was firm in saying that bike lanes in areas like Bloor Street W. is the reason for gridlock and congestion in the city.
"Getting these bike lanes out of the way, restoring vehicle lanes, will allow us to get people moving quicker and faster in one of the busiest cities in the world," he said.
Sarkaria went on to say that he had spoken to "many community members" about the bike lanes. He said their instalment has impacted local business and is causing less people to go downtown.
"We need to restore the vehicle lanes to stop the congestion," he said.

In a separate interview Tuesday with CBC News, Sarkaria said the 600-meter section the province is looking to "immediately" remove along Bloor Street W. would "require the least amount of work" to bring back car lanes.
When asked about how the province will decide to remove or reconfigure the bike lanes it identified, Sarkaria said "the vehicle lane gets the priority."
"In some circumstances where both could coexist, we'll consider that and look at that," he said.
Where will cyclists go if Toronto loses major bike lanes?
When asked about safety concerns once the bike lanes are removed, Sarkaria said the rules of the road will still apply to cyclists and drivers.

"We expect, just like the hundreds of thousands of other streets in Ontario where both the vehicles and cyclists can coexist, that that will continue to happen on the streets that we are specifying right now," he said.
Sarkaria also said secondary streets, such as King Street and College Street, would be better alternatives to the bike lanes the province looks to remove or reconfigure.

items: Ontario aware bike lane removals may not reduce congestion, could make people less safe: internal documents

blocks.text: Internal documents from the transportation ministry that were made public as part of a court challenge to Bill 212 — the legislation that gave the province sweeping control over municipal bike lanes — cast doubt on some of Sarkaria's statements.

Those documents include a report prepared by engineering and urban planning firm CIMA+, which said collisions for all road users could increase upwards of 54 per cent if bike lanes are removed, based on existing research.

A 2024 briefing note on from the cabinet office committee also said the proposed bike lane removals may not achieve "desired outcomes," saying that current data and research "does not confirm that removing bike lanes that occupy a lane of traffic would significantly alleviate congestion."
Ontario appeal court says Ford can rip out Toronto bike lanes
Bike lanes a municipal election issue

Bike lanes are already proving to be a contentious municipal election issue. Mayoral candidate Brad Bradford previously vowed to remove the Bloor Street W. bike lanes should he become mayor, despite initially being one of the councillors who voted in favour of them.

Mayor Olivia Chow, who is seeking re-election this fall, issued a statement Tuesday saying the province should be focused on dealing with Trump and helping families and workers, rather than "picking endless political fights with the City of Toronto."
"I resist any argument that pits road users against each other because it makes everyone less safe. Pedestrians, cyclists and drivers all deserve safety on our roads," Chow said.

items: Tell us what’s at stake for you in Toronto’s municipal election
Bradford vows Bloor Street W. bike lanes are 'coming out' if he's mayor

blocks.text: Mayoral candidate Chris Alexander said the province's actions are evidence of "governance failure" at city hall, and as mayor he'd table a transportation plan that "actually works."

"A competent city works with the province and designs solutions that have neighbourhood support. Toronto needs to get things right the first time, instead of getting stuck in costly court battles for years," Alexander said.
Ontario Green Party leader Mike Schreiner also weighed in on the province's announcement, calling it "performative politics" that "doesn't address the root cause of congestion."
"What we actually need is more dedicated bike and transit lanes and investment in transit that allow for more people to get around more affordably and efficiently," he said in a social media post.
With files from Lane Harrison

articles.title: PH needs 10 to 12 mega food hubs to boost food distribution – DA
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The country needs at least 10 to 12 mega food hubs to help farmers and fisherfolk distribute their goods more efficiently, Agriculture Secretary Francisco Tiu Laurel Jr. said on…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The country needs at least 10 to 12 mega food hubs to help farmers and fisherfolk distribute their goods more efficiently, Agriculture Secretary Francisco Tiu Laurel Jr. said on Tuesday.

During the House committee on appropriations’ briefing on the Department of Agriculture’s (DA) 2027 budget proposal, Tiu Laurel said the agency is eyeing the start of operations of five food hubs during the administration of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.
“From what we can see, the country needs at least 10-12 mega food hubs to lessen traders, increase the profit of farmers… and that will go down to the municipal levels, to public markets,” he said.

The secretary also noted that while Thailand has 16 mega food hubs, the Philippines has none. He said Thailand patterned its food hubs after the concept of Food Terminal Inc., which was originally established during the administration of the late dictator President Ferdinand Marcos Sr.

Tiu Laurel said three food hubs will be implemented under the 2026 national budget in Clark, Pampanga; Isabela; and Pili, Camarines Sur. He added that under the proposed 2027 budget, food hubs are planned for Tiaong, Quezon; San Pablo, Laguna; Albay; Roxas, Zamboanga del Norte; and Manolo Fortich, Bukidnon.

Gabriela Rep. Sarah Jane Elago asked Tiu Laurel if the DA coordinates with the Department of the Interior and Local Government and local government units to help small market vendors secure space in markets even if they can only display their produce weekly or seasonally.

He said the agency continues to implement the Kadiwa ng Pangulo program to link local farmers with different local government units. He noted that there are around 800 Kadiwa sites across the country. /mcm

articles.title: Escudero bars listening devices from VP Duterte impeachment trial
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Witnesses at Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial are prohibited from possessing or accessing earpieces, mobile phones, smartwatches, and similar communication…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Witnesses at Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial are prohibited from possessing or accessing earpieces, mobile phones, smartwatches, and similar communication devices while testifying, Sen. Francis Escudero, the impeachment court presiding officer, warned on Tuesday.

Escudero issued the directive after announcing the court’s finding that a viral image allegedly showing witness Lemuel Ortoni, Office of the Vice President assistant secretary and assistant chief of staff, wearing an earpiece was AI-generated and false.

On Day 20 of the trial, Escudero said he made the announcement, even before the testimony of the next witness, to correct misinformation about Ortonio and to establish a clear rule against coaching or outside influence during testimony.
“After Mr. Ortonio testified before this court, an image of him allegedly wearing an earpiece was widely circulated on the internet,” Escudero said.

“We take this opportunity after verification that it was an AI-generated image and simply false,” he added. “What he had was a front-fold helix, an ear piercing in the front-fold helix of his ear, not an earpiece.”

He did not identify who created or circulated the image but directed the finding to be put on the record to prevent the image from being used as proof of misconduct by Ortonio or any party in the trial.
The false image circulated on social media, suggesting that Ortonio might have been getting coached while on the witness stand.
At the same time, Escudero stressed that the incident required a uniform preventive rule for all succeeding witnesses.
“Every witness must testify solely from his or her own knowledge, free from coaching or influence from counsel or any other person,” he said.
Basis of the directive

According to a House statement on Tuesday, Escudero anchored his directive by analogy to a provision in Supreme Court Administrative Matter No. 24-11-02-SC, which bans the use of cellphones, tablets, and similar gadgets or materials during virtual hearings to prevent coaching and disruption.

Escudero also cited a US Supreme Court case — Villarreal v. Texas — which discussed limits on attorney communications that could shape a witness’s ongoing testimony, including communication through an earpiece while the witness is testifying.

He further cited a 2010 Florida appellate case — Sky Development Inc. v. Vistaview Development Inc. — which involved attempts to influence a witness through a written note and text messages during deposition and trial.
Escudero then enumerated the devices covered by the new directive.

“Accordingly, no witness while testifying shall possess, have access to, or use any earpiece, headset, cell phone, smartwatch, smart glasses, or any other similar device capable of transmitting or receiving information or communication,” he ruled.
The order also applies to any effort to get help from another person while testimony remains unfinished.

“Witnesses are also prohibited from receiving or attempting to receive any communication, suggestion, answer, signal, message, or prompt from any person, whether inside or outside this court, regardless of the means employed,” Escudero said.
“The prohibition shall remain in force during recesses and until the witness is formally discharged by the court,” he added. /atm

articles.title: As glaciers melt, can communities be protected?
articles.summary: Rising temperatures are increasing the risk of floods and avalanches in mountain regions. The disaster in Nepal and Tibet shows the urgent need for solutions, and the tools that could help save lives.

image.caption: Thousands are still missing following last month's devastating floods in Nepal and TibetImage: Sunil Sharma/ZUMA/IMAGO

blocks.text: High mountain glaciers formed in the ice age are retreating and becoming unstable as the burning of fossil fuels heats the climate and leads to a decline in snowfall.
The instability creates the conditions for large glacial sections to collapse, triggering ice and rock avalanches that can dam river valleys before tidal waves of water are released.

Following the glacier collapse that triggered what is know as a mountain tsunami in Nepal and Tibet on August 26, thousands are still missing and feared dead. Unlike the 2025 glacier avalanche that destroyed the town of Batten in Switzerland — where nearly all inhabitants were evacuated — a lack of early warning systems in the Himalayas left locals and tourists at the mercy of flash floods.
How much is climate change to blame?
The causes of glacier collapse are part of a complex web of interrelated changes to high mountain landscapes due in part to rising global temperatures, say scientists.

Levan Tielidze, research fellow in Glacial Geomorphology at Australia's Monash University, says the Himalayas are not, as is often imagined, a "frozen and relatively stable environment," but "dynamic systems in which glaciers, snow, permafrost, rock slopes, rivers and monsoon processes interact."

"As the climate warms, these components are changing simultaneously, meaning hazards can cascade from one process into another," he told DW. When rock, ice and water interact in more unpredictable ways on the world's highest peaks, the resulting debris flows "can transform into a catastrophic flood far downstream," Tielidze added.

Almost 25 years ago, in what was then the biggest glacial collapse in history, one glacier crashed onto another in the Caucases Mountains of North Ossetia in the Russian Federation. The event caused avalanches of ice and debris that slid more than 24km (15 miles) and killed around 125 people.
"The Kolka Glacier disaster was one of the early warnings of the increasing occurrence and potential severity of such glacier-related hazards," Tielidze told DW.
Meanwhile the UN says glaciers in Nepalese mountains have declined by one-third in 30 years, which has added to their instability.

Some research suggests that even if emissions from burning fossil fuels were low enough to prevent the planet from heating by more than 2 degrees Celsius (36 degrees Fahrenheit) compared to pre-industrial times, the wider Hindu Kush Himalayan region could lose up to half its glacier cover — compared to 2020 levels — by the end of the century.

For Dipesh Chapagain, senior scientist at the United Nations University Institute for Environment and Human Security, there is "ample scientific evidence linking greenhouse gas emissions to global climate change, which in turn is driving glacier retreat, permafrost thaw and ice avalanches."
"These changes are increasing both the frequency and intensity of climate-related disasters in mountain regions," he added.

Chapagain has studied hundreds of glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs) in the Hindu Kush Himalaya region — caused when meltwater from glaciers and snow creates a lake that eventually bursts and sends extreme flash floods downstream. The number of these events per decade has increased fivefold since the 1950s.
Pakistani villagers face climate change, melting glaciers

The glacier collapse in Nepal and Tibet shares similarities to a GLOF event; however the former was very different as it skipped the "intermediate lake-formation stage entirely … and directly triggered the flash flood," said Chapagain.

The avalanche also generated seismic activity equivalent to about magnitude 5.2 before the momentum of the water-rich debris flow that entered the river system saw it travel roughly 100 kilometres, noted Tielidze.
"These hazards are becoming so difficult to classify," he added, in reference to the way mountain rock, ice and water are interacting in more unpredictable ways due to climate change.

blocks.caption: Riverside communities in Nepal were destroyed by the unprecedented flash flood and mudslide  Image: Prabin Ranabhat/AFP

blocks.text: Is it possible to adapt to more extreme glacier collapse impacts?

The 2025 glacial collapse in the Swiss Alps that destroyed the entire village of Blattan resulted in one fatality. Detailed surveillance of glacier deformation and the surrounding terrain allowed authorities to evacuate the population before the catastrophic collapse.
But this is less possible in the Hindu Kush Himalaya, which contains more than 63,700 glaciers, notes Tielidze.
"In the Himalayas, we need to move beyond monitoring only individual dangerous lakes," he said.
"We need integrated systems combining satellite observations, seismic detection, glacier and slope monitoring, river gauges, weather forecasts and automated warnings."
For rapidly evolving events such as the Nepal disaster, detecting seismic movement could give downstream communities "precious minutes of warning," he added.

blocks.caption: The destroyed village in Blatten, Switzerland, was in the path of an avalanche of rock, ice, and debris triggered by the collapse of the Birch GlacierImage: Laurent Gillieron/KEYSTONE/picture alliance

blocks.text: Chapagain says the transboundary nature of glacial hazards in the Himalayas makes "cross-border and regional cooperation on disaster preparedness" just as urgent as early-warning systems.
However, currently available adaptation technology and capacity may be insufficient to "respond to a disaster on the scale we've just witnessed on the Bhotekoshi River in Nepal," he added.

"What we have learned from this is we can adapt to climate change but not to climate apocalypse," said Shreya K.C., the Kathmandu-based advocacy working group co-coordinator of the Loss and Damage Youth Coalition, in a statement.
A rapid reduction in planet-heating emissions that are at driving glacial melt and instability will need to accompany any adaptation measures.

"We cannot engineer our way out of unlimited warming," said Tielidze. "Some mountain hazards will remain unpredictable and some changes will eventually exceed the capacity of communities and infrastructure to adapt."

articles.title: Decision on Sara Duterte new trial schedule likely on Sept. 02, 2026 --Tongol
articles.summary: The Senate impeachment court may release on Wednesday, September 2, the ruling on the proposal to adjust the schedule of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte to hasten the…

blocks.text: Published September 1, 2026 9:15pm

The Senate impeachment court may release on Wednesday, September 2, the ruling on the proposal to adjust the schedule of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte to hasten the proceedings, court spokesperson Regie Tongol said.
In a press conference on Tuesday, Tongol said that the trial’s schedule may either be retained, be reverted to the afternoon, or get “mixed.”

“The impeachment court is actually finalizing kung ano po ‘yung actual na changes, if ever na may mangyayari po. As of now, nakuha na ‘yung calendar from the Committee on Finance para makita at ma-plot ng both the Senate President and the Presiding Officer ‘yung mangyayaring possible na schedule,” he explained.

(The impeachment court is finalizing what the actual changes will be, if ever there will be any. As of now, the calendar has been obtained from the Committee on Finance so that both the Senate President and the Presiding Officer can see and plot the possible schedule.)
“Pwedeng mangyari malipat sa hapon totally ‘yung hearing, mag-stay, o kaya naman po mixed —merong mga araw na umaga, may mga araw na hapon,” he added.
(It’s possible that the hearing will be moved to the afternoon entirely, remain as is, or could be mixed —some days it will be in the morning, some in the afternoon.)
Tongol said the impeachment court is considering all options to reach its target of finishing the trial by December this year.
Asked when the new schedule would be disclosed, he said, “Possible tomorrow.”
Tongol said that should the adjusted schedule be announced on Wednesday, its implementation will begin next week.

Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis Escudero earlier said that the court will release a more specific schedule for the impeachment trial once Senate Committee on Finance chairman JV Ejercito comes up with a calendar for the deliberations of the proposed 2027 budget. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Months before ICC trial, Duterte wants prosecution to refile cases vs him
articles.summary: Former president Rodrigo Duterte wants the prosecution to refile a document that 'frames the charges in terms of counts with a defined scope, being crimes under the ICC Statute'

blocks.text: Former president Rodrigo Duterte wants the prosecution to refile a document that 'frames the charges in terms of counts with a defined scope, being crimes under the ICC Statute'

MANILA, Philippines – Just a few months before his scheduled historic trial, former president Rodrigo Duterte asked the International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber III to order the prosecution to refile the cases against him.

“The [defense] accordingly requests the Trial Chamber to order the prosecution to re-file a document before the Pre-Trial Chamber that frames the charges in terms of counts with a defined scope, being crimes under the ICC Statute, and with an exhaustive list of underpinning acts, which represent the entirety of the charges against the accused,” said the Duterte camp’s motion dated August 31.
In the motion, Duterte’s lead counsel Peter Haynes argued that the prosecution’s document containing the charges or DCC “is not fit for [its] purpose” and should be struck out.
This is the Duterte camp’s latest bid to challenge his case before the ICC after recent legal defeats.
Just last April, the ICC pre-trial chamber confirmed all three counts of Duterte’s crimes against humanity case, thus sending him to trial that will start in November.

Even on the issue of jurisdiction or whether the ICC was the right platform for the cases, Duterte did not score a win. The ICC Appeals Chamber junked his jurisdiction challenge and cleared the way for the trial.
The latest defeat was in May, when the pre-trial chamber denied Duterte’s request to appeal the ruling that confirmed his ICC cases.

blocks.caption: ICC denies Rodrigo Duterte’s latest attempt to delay trial

blocks.text: In their August 31 motion, the Duterte camp said the prosecution’s DCC was framed around “illustrative non-exhaustive incidents.” They argued that the way the charges were framed violated Duterte’s right to be informed in detail of the nature, cause, and content of the charges against him under 67(1)(a) of the Rome Statute.
They said the only effective remedy to this is for the prosecution to refile the charges that properly inform Duterte about his case.
According to the defense, the prosecution’s decision to frame the charges that way makes it impossible for Duterte to know what case he has to meet at the upcoming trial.

“The Prosecution’s desire and intention to add further incidents is noteworthy as it plainly indicates that the Prosecution, at least, does not believe that it needs to prove all or most of the incidents. However, with a trial due to start in three months, the [defense] has no idea what is regarded as necessary proof of a ‘count’ on this DCC,” said the motion.
Duterte’s camp further argued that the prosecution’s charge document — which has broad topical headings rather than charged crimes — would allegedly be unacceptable in any criminal jurisdiction.

“The accused cannot even begin to make strategic decisions about how to approach this case, because he does not know what case he has to meet. The Duterte charges are a literal moving target; a non-exhaustive, illustrative list of events whose proof beyond reasonable doubt may or may not trigger liability for thousands of others, and whose evidential value remains entirely unclear,” the camp added. – Rappler.com
