articles.title: On the borderline
articles.summary: With these three novels, we use borderline in both a physical sense and in a metaphorical manner, as the trio of books explores what ‘the other side’ can mean. "Sublimation" by Isabel J. Kim Think of…

blocks.text: With these three novels, we use borderline in both a physical sense and in a metaphorical manner, as the trio of books explores what ‘the other side’ can mean.
"Sublimation" by Isabel J. Kim

Think of the immigrant experience, but now seen through a SciFi lens, and you have an idea of what this novel bravely explores. Kim has written short stories that have won Nebula, Locus, and Shirley Jackson Awards, and this is her debut novel. Soyoung Rose Kang is the protagonist here, and at the age of 10, she left Korea with her mother to emigrate to the USA. She left an ‘instance’ in Korea, who would continue to interact with her family and grandfather. And now, with the death of the grandfather, Soyoung (the instance in Korea) gets in touch with Rose (the instance in the USA), to let her know it was their grandfather’s wish that she come to Seoul for the funeral. What Rose isn’t aware of is that Soyoung harbors the desire to reintegrate. This gets complicated by the fact that the grandfather has left his house to Rose - who never tried to establish a relationship with Soyoung, or her ‘lolo’.

Structured initially so that the chapters alternate between Soyoung and Rose’s POVs, Kim pulls off this delicate balancing act with a lot of skill and charm. She endeavors to make both Soyoung and Rose distinct, while also having such similarities so we appreciate how they are, in fact, two versions of the same person. They’re not twins or doppelgangers, but two ‘instances’-and before the grandfather’s death and meeting in Seoul, have not really been in contact with each other. To make our reading more intense, there’s a Yujin in Korea, and his instance, YJ, in New York. Childhood friend of Soyoung, the Yujin pair have their own set of issues, but have been friends since the moment of ‘instance’, communicating regularly. Their story and how it intersects with that of Soyoung Rose take up the last half of this novel, which takes us to some hard decision-making and the facing of consequences. Bold, imaginative writing that speaks of borders and identity.
"The Pinnacle" by Abir Mukhergee

Set in the penthouse of a luxury condominium called The Pinnacle in Mumbai, this new novel from the author of Hunted, which was named 2025 Thriller of the Year, is both a locked-room mystery thriller and a penetrating study of class dynamics in India today. George Abercrombie is an over-the-hill Hollywood actor who’s married to Sweety Sahota, the current queen of Bollywood. Gemma is Sweety’s PA who joined them in India all the way from the US. The premise has to do with George waking up after a quarrel with Sweety and a drinking binge, and finding her murdered on their king-size bed. With no recollection of what he did the night before, one narrative strand has to do with George having to prove he’s innocent. Then there’s Gemma, who’s receiving cryptic text messages. And finally, there’s Amit, George’s shadow and PA, who seems to know too much and goes on the run.

The seedy underbelly of luxury living is exposed in this gripping adventure. We may be on the 68th floor of an upscale skyscraper, but the hypocrisy, filth, and societal evil still reach these heights. The novel revolves around three plots, and the borders of society and social standing are constantly placed as reminders of what our protagonists have to face on a Daily basis. As in Hunted, Mukhergee is excellent at piling on the action and turning the screws tighter as the novel enters the home stretch. If you’re the type who reads late at night before getting a good night’s sleep, be forewarned that this is a biting thriller, and you’ll be reluctant to put it down, as you’ll be wanting to know what happens next. It’s that well-paced. I would not be surprised if both Hollywood and Bollywood will go bidding for the movie rights to this book; and I know I’ll be looking forward to its film adaptation, and the casting.
"The Lighthouse At the End of the World" by Philip A. Suggars

Think Oliver Twist, but updated for today’s London; then add a spice of portal-esque fantasy - and you’ll have an idea of just how original an adventure this debut novel of Suggars is. It's Charles Dickens meets SciFi, and Oyster McCellan is our scrappy 15-year-old guide to this nifty piece of world-building - two distinct worlds, to be exact. First time we meet Oyster, he’s a member of the Urbans, a small-time gang of grifters who operate around Westminster, hoping to fleece unsuspecting tourists. His father, Lucas, was formerly the head of the gang, but he disappeared without any explanation. So now Oyster has to earn a keep, to help his sister Cecile continue her studies, and their mother Paris, who is still in something of a daze. It’s when a money drop goes terribly wrong that Oyster finds himself in an alternate Greater London.

The novel is familial trauma mixed with immersive world-building. Greater London is a version where leviathans roam the seas, and strangely sympathetic and communicating ink beetles nestle beneath the skin of Oyster’s armpit. Plus there looms the nagging question of whether his father Lucas escaped here, and what his role is in the scheme of things. Meanwhile, as we join Oyster, our tourist guide to Greater London, we encounter the enigma Nonesuch, a female practitioner of rappelling and scavenging skills, the escapist Marya Petrovna who seems to take Oyster under her protective wing but for what deeper purpose, and the terrifying Mr. Primrose, who seems to have his finger on all of Oyster’s movements between worlds, and seems to have confederates from within Oyster’s own gang of Urbans. There’s so much to relish and enjoy as we suspend disbelief and surrender to Suggars' vision and world-building.

articles.title: Haze and air quality index: Things to know
articles.summary: Here's what you should know about air quality indexes and how they help identify the health risks brought by haze

blocks.text: AIR QUALITY. Haze blankets the Metro Manila sky on September 1, 2026, due to smoke from forest fires in Kalimantan, Indonesia. The Manila local government advises residents to take precautions and wear face masks when going outdoors.
Rappler
Here's what you should know about air quality indexes and how they help identify the health risks brought by haze

items: Haze is a form of air pollution caused by smoke, dust, and moisture that can lead to serious health risks, especially for individuals with respiratory diseases.
The Department of Health lists symptoms related to haze exposure, including difficulty breathing, coughing, and chest pains, and advises affected individuals to seek medical attention.
Air quality indexes categorize pollution levels from 'Good' to 'Emergency,' providing guidelines for public safety and recommendations for limiting outdoor exposure during high pollution periods.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – It may look like a harmless fog blanketing the skies, but haze carries small particles in the air that can lead to serious health risks.
Here’s everything you need to know about haze, how to protect yourself from its effects, and how air quality indexes help in measuring risks.
Haze is smoke, dust, moisture, and vapor in the air that affects visibility. It originates from large-scale forest or land fires.
These fires create very fine particles with a diameter of 2.5 micrometers (PM2.5) or smaller that go into the air.
Unlike coarse particles that dissolve in the atmosphere within hours, fine particles can stay in the atmosphere for up to weeks and can travel for hundreds to thousands of kilometers.
These often grow in size as humidity increases and affect air quality by filling the atmosphere with high concentrations of fine particles.
This poses health risks, especially for those with respiratory diseases.
Haze is a form of air pollution that leads to health risks when particles are inhaled.
According to the Department of Health, it could lead to the following:

items: difficulty breathing
coughing
chest pains
watery eyes or excessive tearing
itchy nose
worsening of respiratory disease

blocks.text: The health department advises people experiencing these symptoms to proceed to the nearest health center for treatment.
The Department of Environment and Natural Resources-Environmental Management Bureau (DENR-EMB) reviewed air quality indexes in compliance with the Philippine Clean Air Act of 1999.
In 2020, it formulated the PM2.5 air quality index breakpoints, which are divided into six levels from cleanest to most polluted.
It is used to inform the public about potential health risks.
Below are the air quality indexes, their corresponding colors, and cautions to follow:

items: Good (Green) – air quality is clean and safe
Fair (Yellow) – safe but with a presence of pollution
Unhealthy for sensitive groups (Orange) – people with respiratory disease should limit outdoor exposure

Very Unhealthy (Red) – avoid traffic-heavy areas, and people with respiratory disease should stay indoors and rest as much as possible; trips are encouraged to be postponed, and the use of vehicles is restricted

Acutely Unhealthy (Purple) – people should limit outdoor exposure, and those with respiratory disease should stay indoors and rest as much as possible; unnecessary trips should be postponed, motor vehicle use may be restricted, and industrial activities are limited

Emergency (Maroon) – everyone must stay indoors with windows and doors closed unless heat stress is possible; motor vehicles are only allowed for emergencies, and industrial activities (except those vital for public safety and health) are limited

blocks.text: Here are some tips from the health department to avoid the risks brought by haze:

items: Stay indoors as much as possible.
Wear a KN95 face mask if going outside.
Close all doors and windows and use a wet cloth to cover their crevices.
Use headlights or fog lights when traveling, especially during nighttime.
Stay away from low-lying areas where smoke and suspended particles may settle.

blocks.text: Public events in open areas may continue but must observe air quality before deciding whether to push through or cancel.
Using masks is also encouraged in classrooms, with teachers keeping a close eye on sick students or those with existing heart and lung conditions.
When the haze worsens, vulnerable people (elderly, pregnant, with health conditions) should be stopped from doing long outdoor work. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Manila Water Foundation gives WASH aid to flood-hit communities
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Manila Water Foundation (MWF), together with Manila Water Company’s East Zone and Non-East Zone operating units, activated its Agapay: WASH in Emergencies program to address the…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Manila Water Foundation (MWF), together with Manila Water Company’s East Zone and Non-East Zone operating units, activated its Agapay: WASH in Emergencies program to address the urgent water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) needs of communities affected by flooding brought about by the southwest monsoon or habagat.

In response to severe flooding in Central Luzon caused by continuous monsoon rains, Manila Water Foundation, in partnership with Clark Water and the Municipal Government of San Simon, distributed 600 units of 5-gallon potable drinking water and 200 hygiene kits to evacuees across the municipality.

Each hygiene kit contained essential personal care items, including feminine pads, soap, shampoo, toothpaste, Cleene CLIO toothbrushes, and other hygiene products donated by PHILUSA Corporation. The kits were provided to help evacuees maintain proper hygiene and sanitation while temporarily displaced from their homes.

The flooding significantly affected the Municipality of San Simon, with more than 21,000 families impacted across the town. Among the hardest-hit areas were Barangays San Agustin, San Isidro, San Miguel, Santa Monica, and Sto. Niño, whose residents sought refuge in evacuation centers. Around 500 evacuees from these barangays received hygiene and hydration support through the initiative.
“We recognize that access to clean water and proper sanitation becomes even more critical during emergencies,” said Reginald Andal, Executive Director of Manila Water Foundation.

“Through our Agapay: WASH in Emergencies program, we continue to work closely with our local government and operating unit partners to help protect the health and dignity of affected families. We remain committed to ensuring that vulnerable communities have access to safe water and essential hygiene supplies as they recover from the impacts of disasters. We are also grateful to our partners in local government and the private sector who enable us to respond quickly to the needs of vulnerable families.”

Representatives from the Municipal Government of San Simon expressed their gratitude to Manila Water Foundation and Clark Water for the timely assistance, emphasizing the importance of providing potable water and hygiene products to evacuees. The availability of safe drinking water in evacuation centers helped bring comfort and assurance to affected families during a challenging time.

In the East Zone, MWF, together with the Manila Water Quezon City, Taguig-Pateros, and Rizal Service Areas, provided hydration support for families affected by flooding.A total of 450 units of 5-gallon potable drinking water were handed over to evacuation centers, impacting more than 2,088 evacuees. The LGUs managing the evacuation centers expressed support to Manila Water and MWF, as the safe drinking water supports the health and well-being of children, senior citizens, and other vulnerable community members.
As residents continue to recover, Manila Water Foundation will provide 1,750 gallons of potable drinking water for Barangay San Jose in Rodriguez, Rizal, impacting more than 2,466 individuals.
Manila Water Foundation underscores the vital role of clean water, sanitation, and hygiene in disease prevention and safeguarding public health through Agapay: WASH in Emergencies.

blocks.text: DAVAO CITY — The Department of Agriculture in Davao Region (DA-11) said the ‘Kadiwa on Wheels’ featuring the region’s produce opened at the main office in Quezon City on Tuesday, marking the start of its Metro Manila run.
“There’s durian, mangosteen, pomelo and various other fruits from Davao being displayed,” DA-11 said in a public post.
The initiative aims to bring the region’s harvests closer to consumers in Metro Manila and other parts of the country while expanding market opportunities for farmers.
The DA central office will host the first leg of sales until Sept. 3, followed by ‘Kartilya ng Katipunan’ near the Manila city hall on Sept. 4.
Subsequent stops include Cebu City on Sept. 10 to 16, Baguio City on Sept. 25 to 28, and World Trade Center in Pasay City on Oct. 8 to 10.
DA-11’s Agribusiness and Marketing Assistance Division aims to strengthen market linkages, expand consumer access, and create better opportunities for local growers.
Based on data, the participating farmer cooperatives and associations are the Davao City Durian Industry Development Council and the Durian Industry Association of Davao City.
The target volume of the Kadiwa on Wheels initiative is 70 metric tons. /apl

articles.title: Echoes of cold war as US accused of meddling in another Brazilian election
articles.summary:
Claims that Trump and Rubio are trying to influence result have parallels with CIA intervention 64 years ago

The year was 1962 and the Kennedy administration was desperate to swing Brazil’s…
articles.byline: Tom Phillips in Rio de Janeiro

blocks.text: The year was 1962 and the Kennedy administration was desperate to swing Brazil’s congressional elections against its leftwing president, João Goulart, as a way of countering the supposed communist threat sweeping a region the US considered its back yard.

Historians say that in the lead-up to the vote, the CIA and the Department of State secretly channelled millions of dollars to opposition candidates and a group tasked with spreading rightwing propaganda and stirring up unrest.

blocks.caption: Chico Rubens Paiva, 38, an activist whose grandfather investigated US meddling in Brazilian politics in the 1960s. Photograph: João Laet/The Guardian

blocks.text: “There was a very heavy-handed intervention here by the US government,” said Chico Rubens Paiva, a political activist whose congressman grandfather Rubens Paiva investigated Washington’s meddling during a 1963 parliamentary inquiry into the conspiracy.

More than six decades later, Paiva, whose grandfather was murdered by the US-backed dictatorship that seized power in 1964, is among those who fear history is repeating itself on the eve of Brazil’s 2026 presidential election.

blocks.caption: Rubens Paiva, a civil engineer and politician who was murdered by the military dictatorship in Brazil. Photograph: Family handout

blocks.text: October’s vote will pit the leftwing incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, against the far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro, a Donald Trump ally who is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a military coup.

Polls suggest a tight race and Trump and his secretary of state, Marco Rubio, have been accused of trying to tip the scales in Bolsonaro’s favour by launching an overt campaign of economic and diplomatic pressure against Lula.

The US measures include imposing 25% tariffs on most Brazilian imports and designating Brazil’s biggest crime groups – Rio’s Red Command and São Paulo’s First Command of the Capital – as foreign terrorist organisations. Brazilian officials suspect this is partly designed to boost Bolsonaro by making Lula look soft on crime.

In July, Lula said two Trump officials had been denied entry visas because they planned “to meddle in Brazil’s ​elections”. Brazilian officials believe the pair, who reportedly planned to meet Flávio Bolsonaro, intended to sow doubt about the reliability of Brazil’s internationally respected voting system – something the Bolsonaros have sought to do repeatedly. Soon after, the visa of Brazil’s ambassador to Washington was revoked.

Celso Rocha de Barros, a political scientist and podcast pundit, voiced bewilderment that US interference – which he considered the election’s most urgent theme – was not getting more coverage in mainstream media.

“The greatest superpower in human history is explicitly backing a candidate in our election and is strangling the Brazilian economy in order to help him [win],” Barros claimed. “We cannot pretend that this isn’t happening and treat this like a normal election … the Brazilian economy is under attack.”

Trump’s tactics have echoes of Washington’s cold war-era attempt to manipulate Brazilian politics in the lead-up to the 1964 coup, which ushered in two decades of authoritarian rule in which hundreds of people were killed or disappeared.

Back then, the CIA helped finance the Brazilian Institute for Democratic Action, which, according to the historians Lilia Schwarcz and Heloisa Starling, illegally poured money into the campaigns of hundreds of lawmakers and eight gubernatorial candidates. “The objective was strategic: to create a strong opposition in congress, block government initiatives and prepare the way for a coup d’état,” Schwarcz and Starling argued in their book Brazil: A Biography.

Another US-funded group, the Research and Social Studies Institute, was used to disrupt Goulart’s government by bankrolling anti-communist propaganda and anti-government protests. James N Green, a Brown University historian who has written a book about the period, said: “The intention [was] getting rid of Goulart [and] opening the door to the military coming to power.”

blocks.caption: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, Brazil’s president, at a campaign rally in Rio de Janeiro. The leftwinger faces a tight re-election battle in October. Photograph: Xinhua/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Green sees parallels between Trump’s use of tariffs to sabotage Lula’s campaign and how in the early 60s Washington sought to enfeeble Goulart’s government by funding his opponents and cutting off loans. Then, as now, the US government was “bent on doing everything possible to weaken the government” in Brazil.

But Barros sees one key difference between the two US gambits. “[The 1962 campaign] was done covertly, precisely because the CIA knew there would be real public anger in Brazil if people knew the US was bankrolling candidates. So they did it secretly,” he said. “Today, this is being done openly – and on an incomparably larger scale.”

The Department of State rejected claims the US was seeking to meddle in Brazil’s election. “Any insinuation of a ‘ploy’ to undermine a democratic nation’s election is a baseless lie,” an official said in a statement.

“We respect the Brazilian people and whatever government that they choose freely through free and fair elections in Brazil. We’ve respected and dealt with governments from both sides of the spectrum in Brazil, and had very successful relationships with them.”

Last year Trump was accused of meddling in the politics of neighbouring Argentina after he threw his weight behind its rightwing president, Javier Milei, on the eve of crucial midterm elections. Milei recently attended Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign launch in Brazil, using his speech to lambaste Lula as a “thief”.

blocks.caption: Donald Trump with Marco Rubio in Washington. The pair are accused of waging economic war against Brazil to influence its presidential election. Photograph: Elizabeth Frantz/Reuters

blocks.text: Green believes two strategic objectives lie behind the Brazilian pressure campaign being waged by Trump and by Rubio, the son of Cuban immigrants, who has made toppling Cuba’s communist government a personal project.
Firstly, it is designed to weaken and delegitimise Lula’s government, making it harder for Brazil, Latin America’s largest democracy, to challenge the US economic asphyxiation campaign against Cuba.

Secondly, it is about “neutralising” leftwing forces in Latin America more generally and boosting the right in the hope of helping to elect even more Trump-aligned leaders. Since 2023, a succession of radical rightwing populists have won power in Argentina and Chile, Costa Rica and Colombia. In reference to Trump’s tangerine complexion, this has been nicknamed Latin America’s “orange wave”.

blocks.caption: Paiva is running for a seat in Brazil’s congress in the 2026 elections. Photograph: João Laet/The Guardian

blocks.text: Paiva, 38, believes US interference is intended to have a similar effect to the abduction of Venezuela’s dictator, Nicolás Maduro – strengthening “American dominance” in a region it considers a US sphere of influence.

Maduro’s removal in January allowed the US to impose a pliant successor, his vice-president, Delcy Rodríguez, who has started opening up the South American country to US oil and mining firms. Paiva believes Bolsonaro’s election will “serve the same purpose: putting people into power who will serve their interests”.

He fears that as election day draws near, US social media companies could enter the fray, potentially giving Bolsonaro another lift. “Any kind of change to the algorithm has a brutal impact in the way information reaches people,” warned Paiva, who is running for a seat in congress in the election for the centre-left Brazilian Socialist party. He highlighted “the scary lurch the Silicon Valley bros” had taken into Trump’s camp during his second term.

Barros is convinced the US aims to help elect Flávio Bolsonaro, “because Flávio will give them everything they want”, he said. “Flávio will make a rare earths deal no other president would. Flávio will let American big techs do whatever they like in Brazil. Flávio will reduce economic relations with China as much as he can.” He noted that Bolsonaro supporters attended rallies carrying US flags.

Barros believes the campaign’s real driving force is not Trump but Rubio, who hopes to bolster a possible 2028 presidential run by showing voters he has “delivered the whole of Latin America to American interests”.
“The fact is, this is an election between Lula and Marco Rubio,” Barros said.

articles.title: Why did Modi urge Putin to end Ukraine war - and will he listen?
articles.summary: BBC correspondents in Delhi and Moscow look at why the Indian PM made a very public peace plea to his Russian ally.

blocks.text: If anything, it is very much in line with India's policy of strategic autonomy. Which then begs the question: why would Modi say something on the war so publicly?
The answer lies in the long-standing Russia-India ties - the two countries have generally found a way to work together, even when they see geopolitics through different lenses.
Moscow has continued to be one of India's strongest allies despite Delhi forging closer relationships with Europe and the US in the past three decades.
Delhi is one of the founding members of the Brics grouping of nations along with Russia and China, and it is also a member of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation with the two countries.
But at the same time, Delhi is also a member of the Quad group with Australia, Japan and the US - Moscow has not been happy about this association.
Still, Moscow and Delhi tend to work through these differences. Moreover, Russia still supplies around 40% of India's defence imports and it has also been a steady supplier of Delhi's energy needs.
So, Modi's latest statement is not expected to cause any rift in Moscow-Delhi relations and analysts say it's unlikely that it would have come as a surprise to Putin or his diplomats.
As for the West and Modi's critics in India, they will feel that the prime minister should have been even more direct in his criticism of the war.
This isn't the first time a foreign leader has publicly urged Putin to end the war in Ukraine.
Just five weeks ago the President of Kazakhstan Kassym-Jomart Tokayev suggested Putin freeze the conflict and return to the negotiating table.
He didn't. And he hasn't.
There's no sign of these public calls for peace changing Putin's calculations.
To Modi's call for a cessation of hostilities, the Kremlin leader replied:
"Thank you very much, prime minister. We are moving forward along this path."
Polite, but vague. And non-committal.
After all, a path can be short. But it can also be long. Very long.
And "moving forward" at what pace?
And, crucially, on which path?

All the evidence suggests that Russia's leadership remains convinced it is on a path to military victory in Ukraine. To frame that in terms of peace, "moving forward" to peace on Russia's terms dictated by military success.
Therefore, for now, the fighting goes on.
Despite the fact that, after more than four-and-a-half years of war and huge military losses, the Kremlin has yet to secure victory.

And despite Ukraine's success in bringing the war back home to Russians: for example, through long-range drone strikes on Russian oil refineries that have sparked fuel shortages and petrol queues across the country.

articles.title: Philippines, Nigeria can develop, explore many opportunities — Marcos
articles.summary: The Philippines and Nigeria can explore and develop many opportunities, President Marcos said as he welcomed Nigeria’s new ambassador to the country. Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of…

blocks.text: The Philippines and Nigeria can explore and develop many opportunities, President Marcos said as he welcomed Nigeria’s new ambassador to the country.

Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary of the Federal Republic of Nigeria to the Republic of the Philippines Ibok-Ete Ekwe Ibas presented his Letter of Credence to Marcos at Malacañan Palace on Tuesday, Sept. 1.
During the presentation of credentials, Marcos told the Nigerian envoy that their countries can potentially expand their partnership in energy security, trade, and investment.

"The Philippines and Nigeria have significant potential to expand cooperation especially in energy security, trade and investment, and pursue initiatives that would mutually benefit our peoples and our countries," Marcos said.
"There are many things that, in my view, we can explore and develop. There are so many opportunities that will be of mutual benefit to both our countries," the President added.
"During your tenure as Ambassador, I look forward to further strengthening bilateral relations between our two countries," Marcos also said.
Marcos further said he looks forward to working with the Nigerian ambassador to promote and deepen the Philippines' and Nigeria's collaboration and cooperation, which has spanned 64 years.
Ambassador Ibas, for his part, assured the President that he would work hard to strengthen the friendly, strong bilateral relations between the two countries.
Ibas was joined by his wife and other Embassy officials during the ceremony.
Also present during the event were Foreign Affairs Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro, DFA Assistant Secretary Germinia Aguilar-Usudan, and Deputy Chief of Presidential Protocol Dennis Briones.
The Philippines and Nigeria established diplomatic relations on August 1, 1962, and will mark 65 years of diplomatic relations in 2027.

articles.title: Severe offenders face exclusion: DepEd tightens penalties for bullying, violence, threats in schools
articles.summary: Learners who commit severe acts of bullying, physical assault, or threats may face immediate exclusion, non-readmission, and mandatory referral to law enforcement or social welfare authorities under…

blocks.text: (PHOTO: PIXABAY)

Learners who commit severe acts of bullying, physical assault, or threats may face immediate exclusion, non-readmission, and mandatory referral to law enforcement or social welfare authorities under stricter Department of Education (DepEd) rules.

This was the agency’s warning as it formalized consolidated learner protection protocols under DepEd Order No. 006, s. 2026, or the Guidelines on Ensuring a Safe and Motivating Learning Environment (ESMLE).

According to DepEd, its campaign against violence and classroom disruptions is being implemented in coordination with partner agencies, local government units (LGUs), law enforcement authorities, and local communities.
While learners deserve an opportunity to change, Angara said DepEd would never put the safety of the majority at risk.
“Ang paaralan ay dapat maging ligtas at tahimik na lugar para sa lahat (Schools should be safe and peaceful places for everyone),” he said in a statement.
The education department said severe offenses will prompt immediate inter-agency action under the policy.

“Grounded in a whole-of-society framework, the guidelines mandate direct coordination between school administrations, the Philippine National Police (PNP), the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD), LGUs, and communities to address safety threats both on-site and online,” it said.

Per DepEd, a school’s Child Protection Committee must immediately investigate any reported bullying incident or safety threat, secure the victim’s safety, and provide affected learners with mental health and psychosocial support.
“The policy enforces a progressive disciplinary framework depending on the severity of the offense,” the agency stated.
DepEd said first-level or minor infractions will result in a written reprimand, parental notification, and guidance counseling.

“Second-level or serious offenses such as repeated bullying and online harassment result in an immediate suspension of up to five days and mandatory DSWD referral, escalating to non-readmission on the second offense, and full exclusion on the third,” it added.

Meanwhile, the agency said third-level or high-risk acts, including those involving severe physical harm, bomb threats, or dangerous hoaxes, will result in non-readmission for the first offense and permanent exclusion for the second, as well as immediate turnover to law enforcement authorities.
“School heads are also authorized to issue a 30-day preventive suspension during ongoing investigations if a learner poses a continuing risk to campus safety,” it stated.
As such, DepEd said it has streamlined the response to bullying incidents, with teachers tasked to directly handle and resolve conduct considered a precursor to bullying.

“For Second-level offenses that cause harm to other learners and stakeholders, the Learner Formation Officer intervenes and provides recommendations to the school head, as the case may be,” the agency said.
“A Third-level offense is resolved by the School Head who also imposes the appropriate sanction. At all levels, the parents of the learner-offender are informed.”
DepEd stressed that aside from administrative sanctions, offenders referred to external authorities may face criminal liability or custodial intervention, depending on the offense.
Angara warned that DepEd would strictly enforce the measures to uphold its zero-tolerance policy against violence and disruption.

"Kung ang isang estudyante ay gagamit ng dahas, mananakit, magdadala ng patalim o baril, mag-aaksaya ng oras sa paggawa ng bomb threat jokes o pranks, o patuloy na mambubully ng kaklase, hindi natin ito papalampasin (If a student resorts to violence, harms others, brings a knife or firearm, makes bomb threats as jokes or pranks, or repeatedly bullies a classmate, we will not let it pass),” he said.

“Ipatutupad natin ang pinakamabigat na parusa kabilang ang pagpapatalsik sa paaralan at direktang pag-turnover sa mga awtoridad (We will impose the most severe penalties, including expulsion from school and direct turnover to the authorities),” he added.
Under non-readmission, an offender may finish the current academic year but cannot re-enroll the following year, DepEd said.
Exclusion, meanwhile, immediately removes the learner from the school’s active rolls, with education continuing only through alternative interventions.

articles.title: DSWD distributes over P618.3M in aid to flood-hit Central Luzon
articles.summary: The Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) has distributed over P618.3M worth of assistance to individuals affected by flooding in Central Luzon, Malacañang said Tuesday.

blocks.text: Published September 1, 2026 7:37pm
The Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) has distributed over P618.3M worth of assistance to individuals affected by flooding in Central Luzon, Malacañang said Tuesday.

“Ayon sa ulat ni Social Welfare and Development Secretary Rex Gatchalian, umabot sa mahigit P618.3 million na halaga ng humanitarian assistance ang naihatid sa mga apektadong lalawigan sa Central Luzon gaya ng Tarlac, Pampanga at Bulacan,” Palace Press Officer Undersecretary Claire Castro said in a press briefing.

(According to Social Welfare and Development Secretary Rex Gatchalian, more than P618.3 million worth of humanitarian assistance has been delivered to affected provinces in Central Luzon, including Tarlac, Pampanga, and Bulacan.)

“Sa buong Region III naman ay umaabot sa mahigit 874.8 million pesos ang halaga ng naipaabot na tulong. Kasama sa mga interventions ang pamamahagi ng family food packs, ready-to-eat foods, non-food items at AICS,” she added.

(Across Region III, more than P874.8 million worth of assistance has been provided, including family food packs, ready-to-eat food, non-food items, and aid through the Assistance to Individuals in Crisis Situation (AICS) program.)
Castro further reported that DSWD also deployed its specialized disaster response vehicle and three mobile kitchens to the affected areas.

The Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) earlier said it had deployed troops, military vehicles, and water assets to flood-hit areas in Luzon, while disaster response teams were sent to Tarlac, Pampanga, and Bataan to deliver aid.—LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Germany's center-left SPD is fighting for survival
articles.summary: The Social Democratic Party is sinking ever deeper into crisis. Voters are turning away, while unrest is growing within its grassroots ranks. Will upcoming state elections accelerate the party's…

image.caption: SPD chairpeople Bärbel Bas and Lars Klingbeil have seen support for their party dwindleImage: Kay Nietfeld/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: At a fitness class run by the Workers' Welfare Association, one stop on his tour through Saxony-Anhalt, Matthias Miersch is giving it his all: Hands up, hands down, touch your toes, all in time to the German schlager hit "Regenbogenfarben."
Miersch, leader of the center-left Social Democratic Party's (SPD) parliamentary group, has traveled to Saxony-Anhalt for a 24-hour visit to lend his support.

The election campaign in the eastern German state has entered its decisive final phase. In the state capital, Magdeburg, and three smaller towns, Miersch meets with SPD state politicians and local residents. He takes part in discussions with a queer advocacy organization, a housing cooperative and an initiative dedicated to the social integration of young refugees.

Everything revolves around the party's core issues: affordable housing, social support, poverty reduction, integration and protection against discrimination based on sexual identity. At the Rainbow Cafe in Magdeburg, Miersch speaks openly about his own sexual identity as a gay man. Those gathered there describe the open hatred and hostility they encounter, especially in rural areas, and speak of their growing fear of the prospect of a state government led by the Alternative for Germany (AfD).
The AfD's Saxony-Anhalt branch has been classified by the domestic intelligence agency as a confirmed right-wing extremist organization.

"We are witnessing a rollback of the freedoms and lifestyles that have emerged over recent decades," Miersch said at the cafe. The small room is colorful and crowded; a nearby shelf is decorated with small flags bearing the slogan "No Time for Nazis."
SPD cannot stop the AfD
The Social Democrats have little with which to counter the AfD's rise in Saxony-Anhalt. Germany's oldest political party is polling at just 7 to 8%, compared to the AfD's 42%.

The SPD's main concern is that it might even fall below the 5% threshold for representation in parliament. The reason for the dwindling support is that many voters feel the party — the junior coalition partner in the deeply unpopular federal government alongside the center-right Christian Democratic Union and Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) — no longer has a clearly defined identity.
"I do not want to conceal the fact," Miersch told journalists traveling with him at the end of the tour, "that federal politics is also fueling debate here on the ground."

What he is referring to above all is the planned reform of the statuary pension system, especially the proposal to abolish the option of early retirement after 45 years, often referred to as retirement at 63. For many residents of Saxony-Anhalt, which has long grappled with an aging population and demographic decline, the proposal is a particularly contentious issue.
Elections in five federal states
Yet Saxony-Anhalt is not the only place where the SPD is battling decline. Nationwide, the party is polling at only around 12%, trailing the AfD, the CDU/CSU and the Greens.

The situation is even more acute in some individual states. With elections in five of Germany's 16 states and city-states, 2026 is a super election year. Two of those contests have already taken place.

The results so far are sobering: in the southwestern state of Baden-Württemberg, the SPD recorded its worst result of the postwar era and only just managed to retain its representation in the state parliament. In Rhineland-Palatinate, after 35 years in power, the party was decisively pushed into second place by the CDU. Its election result there was the worst in the state's history.

September now threatens to bring further setbacks, and not only in Saxony-Anhalt. In the city-state of Berlin, the party is languishing in fifth place at just 12%, while in the eastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania it could face the same fate as in Rhineland-Palatinate: a loss of power.
Frustration growing within SPD

An increasing number of Social Democrats are speaking of an existential crisis. The once-proud workers' party, which at its peak could count every second voter among its supporters, now faces the prospect of political irrelevance.
"I see a party that is dying," Berlin state legislator Orkan Özdemir, co-chair of the SPD's Working Group on Migration and Diversity, told the German Press Agency in early August.
In a letter to the party executive, the group's leadership called for a special party conference this autumn and a restructuring of the party leadership. They are far from alone in doing so.

Dissatisfaction, which first surfaced after the SPD's initial two state election defeats, is now spreading throughout the party. This comes at a particularly difficult moment, with the SPD in the midst of an election campaign and, in principle, expected to project unity.
Painful compromise over social, migration policies

At the heart of the criticism is the dual role of party leaders Bärbel Bas and Lars Klingbeil, who also serve as members of the federal government. Critics argue that the arrangement is simply not working.
As labor minister and finance minister, respectively, they are seen as doing too little alongside CDU Chancellor Friedrich Merz to give the SPD a distinct political profile of its own.
German regional vote reveals economy worries and SPD decline

Too many concessions, particularly on social policy, have been made to the CDU, critics contend: cuts to housing benefits, the abolition of Germany's "retirement at 63" provision, and the requirement to provide a doctor's note from the first day of illness.

The party is also facing headwinds over its tougher migration policy. Those calling for a special party conference argue that a long-overdue debate is needed over whether the government's course still reflects the party's own principles and policy positions.
Challenge for party leaders Bas, Klingbeil
The question of what the SPD still stands for, whom it represents and what it should support in the future is increasingly becoming a matter of the party's very survival.

"We have lost the trust of voters because, on many issues, the SPD was unwilling to ruffle feathers," Bas said after the first two state elections this year. "In some cases, we have also failed to communicate clearly. Many people no longer know what the SPD stands for."

Klingbeil has also expressed understanding for the critics, though he remains unfazed. It is perfectly normal for issues to be debated within the party, he said during a campaign appearance in Saxony-Anhalt.
"We're at 12% nationwide, and these are extraordinarily turbulent times. I know that some of the decisions made at the federal level are demanding a great deal from my own party, too," he said.
Workers voting for the AfD

According to an analysis by the polling institute Forsa published in November 2025, only 9% of blue-collar workers and unemployed voters would now choose the SPD. Those who feel socially disadvantaged today are increasingly drawn to the AfD. In February 2025, pollsters at infratest dimap published figures showing that 38% of workers were voting for the AfD.
For the SPD, that is a sobering finding.

More and more Social Democrats see their party at a turning point. They are calling on the SPD to find its way back to a clearly recognizable political profile, if necessary even from the opposition benches.
Otherwise, they fear, the party could be crushed between the demands of governing, internal factional struggles and the loss of its former core electorate.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Palace: Marcos did not serenade First Lady during height of Habagat
articles.summary: The Palace on Tuesday clarified that President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. did not sing a serenade to First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos at the height of the Southwest Monsoon rains that flooded many…

blocks.text: Published September 1, 2026 7:36pm

The Palace on Tuesday clarified that President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. did not sing a serenade to First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos at the height of the Southwest Monsoon rains that flooded many parts of the country.

In a video from former Vigan City mayor Jose Singson Jr., Marcos could be seen greeting his wife and serenading her. The video has garnered negative reactions from netizens, with many criticizing Marcos for seemingly partying as the country reeled from the effects of the Habagat.
However, Palace Press Officer Claire Castro said that this was not the case.
“Naganap po ang pagharana ng Pangulo, kay First Lady, hindi po ito iyong kasagsagan noong malakas na ulan, hindi po ito kasagsagan ng pagbaha,” Castro said on Tuesday.
(The serenade from the President, for the First Lady, is not during the height of the strong rains, it was not during the height of the floods.)
Castro said the narrative was twisted by detractors and obstructionists. She said the video was taken in the evening, when Marcos had already wrapped up his duties for the day.
However, she said it was understandable why some people would see the gesture as insensitive if this was the narrative that they were fed.
“Kung nagharana man ang Pangulo, para sa kanyang asawa at mga kasama ang ilang malalapit na kamag-anak, kaunting oras lang po ang ibinigay ng Pangulo, para sa kanyang pamilya,” Castro said.
(If the President did sing, this is for his wife and a few close family members, it is just a few hours given by the President for his family.) —RF, GMA News

articles.title: 2027 budget: P16B for farm-to-market roads insufficient – DA
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The proposed P16 billion for the construction and rehabilitation of farm-to-market road (FMR) projects for 2027 is insufficient to cover the thousands of kilometers needed under…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The proposed P16 billion for the construction and rehabilitation of farm-to-market road (FMR) projects for 2027 is insufficient to cover the thousands of kilometers needed under the system, Agriculture Secretary Francisco Tiu Laurel said on Tuesday.

During the House committee on appropriations’ briefing on the proposed budget of the Department of Agriculture (DA), Tiu Laurel said 55,000 kilometers (km) are needed under the FMR system as of Aug. 31, 2026.
“With the limited budget of P16 billion, we can’t achieve that,” he added.

He explained that under the 2027 National Expenditure Program (NEP), the DA’s FMR projects were allotted P16 billion. This is a more than 50 percent decrease from the P33,009,763,000 budget allotted for the projects in the 2026 national budget.
“It’s difficult to implement that because we are only given P16 billion for 55,000 km,” he added.
Tiu Laurel noted that the proposed budget for the FMR projects was determined by the fiscal allocation given to the agency under the NEP.
In the same hearing, Rep. Robert Nazal asked if the DA uses a scientific database to identify areas to be prioritized under the FMR projects.

Tiu Laurel said the DA uses parameters such as road influence area, poverty incidence, number of farmer or fisherfolk beneficiaries, present road conditions, climate change adaptation, average daily traffic, and new production areas, among others.

Nazal then asked the secretary if the agency considers areas where it can observe a return on investment. The secretary said that while this is a general practice, the agency also determines areas with “missionary roots,” with little production but high potential for benefits later on.
More scrutiny

Showing the FMR transparency portal in his presentation, Rep. Antonio Tinio pointed out the completed projects out of the total projects indicated. He asked Tiu Laurel why the agency had completed only half of the total projects.

Based on the transparency portal of FMR infrastructure projects from 2021 to 2026, 3,235 projects were completed out of the 6,428 total projects, with a total investment of P109.53 billion. The completed projects spanned 2,485.23 kilometers.
Tiu Laurel said the projects allocated for 2026 have not yet been implemented because the Special Allotment Release Order was released by the Department of Budget and Management only last week.
He added that of the P23 billion budget for FMR projects in 2025, only P12 billion was released to the agency. /mcm

articles.title: House leaders honor Speaker Dy on 65th birthday
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — House leaders paid tribute to Speaker Faustino “Bojie” G. Dy III on his 65th birthday on Tuesday, praising his “steady, inclusive, and results-driven leadership” in…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — House leaders paid tribute to Speaker Faustino “Bojie” G. Dy III on his 65th birthday on Tuesday, praising his “steady, inclusive, and results-driven leadership” in strengthening and restoring public trust in the lower chamber.

In a surprise birthday activity organized by House officials and staff, Senior Deputy Speaker Rep. Ferdinand “Dinand” Hernandez of South Cotabato praised Dy, saying: “I have always believed in your sincerity, determination, and unwavering commitment to introduce meaningful change in Congress, even when the decisions were difficult, and the challenges seemed overwhelming. You stood your ground, ushered in a new normal, and helped restore the public’s trust in the institution.”

“You have quietly and steadily done the job, never seeking the spotlight, and let the results speak for themselves — Congress has delivered a remarkable performance and continues to do so under your watch,” Hernandez added.
Hernandez also thanked Dy for the trust and friendship they developed in Congress.

“I’m proud to call you my Speaker, my boss, my mentor, and most importantly, my friend. I will always be grateful for your friendship, guidance, and most of all, the trust you have placed in me. God bless you always! Together with my constituents from the 2nd District and the Province of South Cotabato, we wish you a happy birthday, Boss Bojie!” he added.
Majority Leader Ferdinand Alexander “Sandro” Marcos of Ilocos Norte also thanked Dy for his leadership and for helping him fulfill his responsibilities.
Marcos credited the speaker for rallying members of the House and keeping the chamber united and focused on performing its constitutional mandate for the people.
For Minority Leader Marcelino Libanan, Dy’s ability to work with lawmakers across political lines is rooted in both his character and his long experience in public service.
“Napakabuting tao,” Libanan said of Dy.
(“A very good person.”)

Libanan noted Dy’s being in public service for four decades, beginning as a barangay chair and eventually rising to become House speaker, attributing his longevity to “competence, hard work, and humility.”

He also credited Dy with taking the helm of the House at a difficult period when public ratings of the institution had declined, and successfully steering the chamber toward improved public trust and approval ratings.
Meanwhile, House Secretary General Cheloy E. Velicaria-Garafil called Dy “the best Speaker in the history of the House,” citing in particular his genuine concern for the welfare of House employees.

Visibly moved by the surprise celebration, Dy thanked his House colleagues and staff for their support, saying: “Sa amin sa probinsya, laging pinagmamalaki namin yung unity — pagkakaisa natin — regardless kung ano yung paniniwala natin, kung ano yung ating posisyon sa buhay… pero pagdating sa trabaho, pagdating sa kabutihan ng mas nakakarami, nagsasama-sama tayo para diyan.”

(“In our province [Isabela], we’ve always been proud of unity — our unity — regardless of what we believe, of what our station in life is… but when it comes to work, when it comes to what’s good for the majority, we joined together for that.”)
“Palakasin pa natin yung ating paniniwala na kayang-kaya nating ibangon ang Bagong Kongreso,” he added.
(“Let us strengthen our trust that we can easily raise the Bagong Kongreso [New Congress],”) /atm

articles.title: Duterte’s defense team asks ICC to order prosecutors to refile charges
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Former President Rodrigo Duterte’s defense team has asked the International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber III to order prosecutors to “refile” the charges against him. The…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Former President Rodrigo Duterte’s defense team has asked the International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber III to order prosecutors to “refile” the charges against him.
The defense panel believes the prosecution violated the former president’s “right to be informed in detail of the nature, cause and content of the charges.”

Based on a copy of the motion dated Aug. 31, 2026, signed by lead defense counsel Peter Haynes, the defense pointed out how the framing of the charges against Duterte departed from previous cases before the ICC.

According to the defense, instead of containing a “clear set of settled facts and circumstances supporting separate counts,” the document containing the charges (DCC) was framed around “illustrative non-exhaustive incidents, grouped under topical headings.”

“For the reasons set out herein, the Defence submits that the charges, as currently framed, violate the accused’s right to be informed in detail of the nature, cause and content of the charges against him under Article 67(1)(a) of the Statute,” the motion read.

“The only effective remedy would be for the Prosecution to be ordered to re-file a set of charges that properly informs the accused of the case he needs to meet, pursuant to Article 61(9) of the Statute,” it added.
Duterte is facing three counts of crimes against humanity due to his administration’s war against illegal drugs.
The campaign reportedly killed at least 6,000 people based on government records, and over 30,000 based on some human rights groups’ reports.
The victims allegedly include children as young as 3-years-old. /apl

articles.title: Joel Villanueva: NLEx should refund toll fees for stranded motorists
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Sen. Joel Villanueva on Tuesday urged the management of the North Luzon Expressway (NLEx) to consider waiving or refunding toll fees paid by motorists who were stranded for…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Sen. Joel Villanueva on Tuesday urged the management of the North Luzon Expressway (NLEx) to consider waiving or refunding toll fees paid by motorists who were stranded for hours amid severe flooding along NLEx in San Simon, Pampanga.

In his privilege speech before the Senate, Villanueva also called for a clear, funded and permanent solution to the recurring flooding that has repeatedly disrupted traffic along the major expressway.
“Naniniwala rin tayo na dapat ikonsidera ng NLEx management ang pag-waive o pag-refund ng toll fees para sa mga motoristang matinding naapektuhan ng prolonged closure,” Villanueva said.
(We also believe that the NLEx management should consider waiving or refunding toll fees for motorists severely affected by the prolonged closure.)
“Nagbayad ka na ng toll, naipit ka pa sa baha. Hindi po iyon ang serbisyong binayaran ng ating mga kababayan,” he added.
(You already paid the toll, only to get stuck in the flood. That is not the service our fellow Filipinos paid for.)
Villanueva made the statement amid reports that traffic along the affected portion of NLEX stretched as far as 10 kilometers, with some motorists reportedly spending up to 22 hours on the road.
He also asked NLEx whether immediate assistance had been provided to stranded motorists.
“May tubig, pagkain, portalets, at medical assistance po ba para sa mga nangangailangan?” he said.
(Were there water, food, portalets, and medical assistance to those affected?)
Villanueva stressed that the situation should not be treated as a simple inconvenience, given the prolonged period motorists were trapped on the expressway.
“Usapin po ito ng kaligtasan at kapakanan ng tao,” he said.
(This is a matter of safety and welfare of the people,)
The Inquirer sought a comment from NLEx on the matter but has yet to receive a response as of posting time.

Meanwhile, the Metro Pacific Tollways Corporation, operator of NLEx, has previously expressed its apologies to motorists who have been stranded in some sections of the expressway, which were rendered impassable because of severe flooding.
Recurring problem
Villanueva noted that the flooding in San Simon was not a new problem.

He recalled that following a similar flooding incident in 2023, the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) and NLEx identified the construction of the Tulaoc Overpass and the raising of portions of the expressway as a medium-term solution.
Since then, NLEx has raised a 0.7-meter section of a 200-meter stretch in the Tulaoc area, the senator noted.
But Villanueva said it was clear that simply raising the road was not enough to address the recurring flooding.
He also acknowledged that there were limitations to raising the expressway further because of existing bridges and required vehicle clearances.
While pumping equipment is being used to remove floodwaters, Villanueva said this should only be considered an emergency response, rather than a permanent solution.
‘Critical economic lifeline’
Villanueva described NLEx as a “critical economic lifeline,” noting that the expressway handled an average of more than 350,000 vehicle entries every day in 2024, according to NLEx Corporation.
“Kapag naparalisa ang NLEx, apektado ang trabaho, negosyo, supply chain, at oras ng ating mga kababayan,” Villanueva said.
(When NLEx is paralyzed, jobs, businesses, the supply chain, and the time of our fellow Filipinos are affected.)

He also raised concerns over the rerouting of motorists to the Central Luzon Link Expressway (CLLEx) and the Subic-Clark-Tarlac Expressway (SCTEx). Villanueva said there were insufficient signs, traffic personnel, lighting, and clear directions to guide motorists through alternative routes.
He also noted that navigation apps may not immediately reflect road closures, potentially leaving motorists unaware of the flood.
“Sa emergency, information is also a form of assistance. Hindi dapat makarating muna ang motorista sa baha bago niya malaman na hindi pala siya makakadaan dito,” he said.
(In an emergency, information is also a form of assistance. Motorists should not have to reach the flooded area before finding out that they cannot pass through)
Beyond emergency measures, however, Villanueva said authorities should pursue a “clear, funded, time-bound, and permanent solution” to the recurring flooding in San Simon.
“Our people deserve an expressway that is not only fast when the weather is good, but safe, reliable, and resilient when they need it most,” Villanueva said. /mr

articles.title: DA seeks bigger 2027 budget for palm oil industry
articles.summary: The Department of Agriculture (DA) on Tuesday said it is seeking an additional budget for the palm oil industry next year, citing the country"s heavy dependence on imports.

blocks.text: Published September 1, 2026 7:27pm
The Department of Agriculture (DA) on Tuesday said it is seeking an additional budget for the palm oil industry next year, citing the country’s heavy dependence on imports.

“We are importing almost 90% of our palm oil requirement... We definitely need to allocate funds for that," DA Secretary Francisco Tiu Laurel Jr. said during a House briefing on the department’s proposed P198-billion budget for next year.

“Because it was not substantially included in our National Expenditure Program since we only saw the actual need in the last two months. So we are requesting a special provision for palm oil, with an additional P500 million for next year,” he added.
Tiu-Laurel said he had spoken with Senator Kiko Pangilinan and Congressman Mark Enverga to request additional funding for the palm oil industry.
"In the following years, hopefully, if there is a law, P1 billion can be allocated for it every year for the next five years," he said.
For this year, the proposed P1 billion allocation for the palm oil industry was slashed by 92.1% to just P79 million.

DA data showed that oil palm has an average yield of 3.8 metric tons per hectare, compared with less than one metric ton for coconut. As a result, palm oil farmers earn more than twice as much annually as coconut farmers, who earn an average of about P90,000.
Of the 100,000 hectares planted with oil palm nationwide, most are in Mindanao.

Last February, the DA said it was considering the University of Southern Mindanao in Kabacan, North Cotabato, as a base for reviving and scaling up a government-backed nursery that would provide high-quality, disease-free planting materials sourced from Malaysia.

“Our idea, based on the roadmap we have identified, is that we need to plant 300,000 hectares of palm oil. If we can reach 100,000 hectares by the end of 2028, that would be very good,” Tiu Laurel said during the budget hearing.
Reorganize PCA?

As part of efforts to boost the country’s palm oil industry, Tiu Laurel said the DA is considering reorganizing the Philippine Coconut Authority (PCA) to create a dedicated team that would handle the palm oil sector.

“If it is a matter of the authority, what is important is that we establish an agency or reorganize the PCA so that it is not just a coconut authority. It could have a deputy administrator specifically for palm oil and another specifically for coconut, each with their own teams,” he said.
The TUCP Party-list has filed a bill seeking to develop the Philippine palm oil sector. The measure remains pending at the committee level.
Tiu Laurel said he would ask President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. to certify the measure as urgent.
“The DA definitely supports the certification of the palm oil bill as urgent and I will make my official recommendation tomorrow to the President,” he said.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Comelec seeks bigger budget for 2027 as it prepares for 2028 elections
articles.summary: Speaking at a House budget hearing, Comelec Chairman George Garcia says P9.12 billion was cut from the poll body's budget for preparation for the national and local elections

blocks.text: ELECTIONS. Voters cast their vote at polling precincts of Guadalupe Elementary School in Cebu City, in the midterm elections, on May 12, 2025.
Jacqueline Hernandez/Rappler
Speaking at a House budget hearing, Comelec Chairman George Garcia says P9.12 billion was cut from the poll body's budget for preparation for the national and local elections

items: The Commission on Elections requested a P52.66-billion budget for 2027, but the Department of Budget and Management recommended only P44.7 billion.
Comelec Chairman George Garcia warned that budget cuts totaling P9.12 billion could compromise election preparations, leading to a shortage of election counting machines and longer voting times.

The proposed budget also lacks funding for essential operations, including ballot printing and venue leasing for the filing of certificates of candidacy, which the Comelec aims to hold earlier in September 2027.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – The Commission on Elections (Comelec) on Tuesday, September 1, appealed to the House of Representatives to restore its proposed P52.66-billion budget request for 2027.

The Comelec requested a higher budget in preparation for the national and local elections in 2028. The Department of Budget and Management (DBM), however, only recommended a P44.7-billion budget for the poll body in 2027.
Speaking at a House budget hearing, Comelec Chairman George Garcia said P9.12 billion was cut from the Comelec’s budget for preparation for the national and local elections.
He warned that the cuts could compromise the poll body’s preparations if the budget proves insufficient.
The Comelec estimated that there would be around 74 million voters by 2028, which would also increase the demand for a higher number of voting precincts.
The DBM also slashed P5.75 billion from the Comelec’s proposed budget for regular operations and P345 million from its other locally funded projects.

If the budget cuts were not restored by Congress, the Comelec said there would be a shortage of 9,310 election counting machines. This could increase the number of voters assigned to each polling precinct, resulting in longer lines and voting times on election day.

Garcia said the cuts would also affect the printing of ballots, forms, and voter information sheets, as well as the deployment of machines and supplies to polling places. Other affected expenses include ballot packaging, consultancy for an international certification entity, and overtime pay.

The DBM also removed the P118-million budget proposal of the Comelec for the lease of warehouses and venues. Without this, Garcia said they will not have a venue for the filing of certificates of candidacy in September 2027.
The filing of certificates of candidacy is typically held in October, but the Comelec wants to set the filing period from September 20 to 27, 2027.
The Comelec said an earlier filing of certificates of candidacy will allow the poll body to print ballots earlier.

The 2027 budget proposal also contains no allocation for the Comelec’s capital outlay, which covers physical assets such as buildings. Garcia said the commission’s lack of adequate office space has long been a problem. – Rappler.com

blocks.text: Despite several postponements, the first parliamentary elections in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) will push through, President Marcos affirmed.
The government, Marcos said, is prepared to finally make it happen.

"We are prepared for the first parliamentary elections in the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao on September 14th," Marcos said during the opening ceremony of the 2026 National Peace Consciousness Month on Tuesday, Sept. 1.
"Despite several postponements, the government never lost hope and remains fully committed to supporting this democratic exercise," he added.
The Chief Executive assured the Bangsamoro region that the administration will ensure the upcoming polls will be held peacefully.
"Be assured that this administration will do everything within our mandate to ensure that the elections are safe, peaceful, and credible," Marcos said.

"We will protect the right of every Bangsamoro voter to cast a ballot freely and without fear. Let this election show that the future of the Bangsamoro is shaped by the people themselves, through your voices, your choices, and your hopes for your respective communities," he added.
Marcos also said that the election in Bangsamoro is "another opportunity to show that the gains of peace can be strengthened through democratic institutions."
Peace must be chosen, lived, strengthened
In his speech, the President underscored that "peace entails responsibility," urging the citizenry to always choose to be at peace with fellow Filipinos.
"It must be chosen. It must be lived, protected, and strengthened every single day," he said.
Marcos stressed that every Filipino has a role to play in strengthening peace in the country, emphasizing that "peace is the seed of progress."

"Let us always choose to be at peace with our fellow Filipinos. Just like any family, we may have different and disagreeing views. However, we remain bound by something much stronger than our differences," he said.
"We share one home. We share one future. We share one Filipino identity," he added.

articles.title: Lubang launches research, documentation of Balsehan in Oriental Mindoro
articles.summary: CALAPAN CITY, Oriental Mindoro — The municipal government of Lubang in Oriental Mindoro has launched a research and documentation project aimed at preserving the history, movements, music, costumes…

blocks.text: CALAPAN CITY, Oriental Mindoro — The municipal government of Lubang in Oriental Mindoro has launched a research and documentation project aimed at preserving the history, movements, music, costumes and cultural significance of the Balsehan ng Lubang, a traditional cultural practice closely associated with the island town’s Mayohan Festival.

The project is being undertaken by the Lubang Municipal Tourism Office and the Municipal Tourism, Culture and the Arts Council (MTCAC), which are seeking the participation of residents, cultural practitioners and community elders who can provide information and historical materials about the tradition.
The local government said the Balsehan is more than a traditional dance or festival performance. It reflects the town’s history, faith, identity, music, traditions and collective memory.

However, much of the knowledge about the Balsehan has yet to be recorded and remains preserved largely through the memories and experiences of elders and cultural bearers, according to the tourism office.

The research team is collecting old photographs, videos, audio recordings, musical instruments, costumes, festival programs, newspaper clippings and other documents related to the Balsehan and Mayohan Festival.

It is also seeking information about former Balsehan dancers, choreographers, musicians, trainers, cultural bearers and elders who may provide accounts about the tradition’s origins, development and continued practice.
As part of the project, researchers conducted interviews and gathered information from residents of Barangay Maliig on Aug. 31.

The fieldwork focused on collecting community narratives, knowledge and personal experiences that could help establish the history and origins of the Balsehan and document how the tradition has evolved over the years.

The tourism office said every story, recollection and piece of information contributed by community members forms part of the effort to preserve and strengthen the Balsehan as an important part of Lubang’s cultural heritage and identity.
Residents who have old photographs, recordings, documents, memorabilia or other materials related to the Balsehan are encouraged to share them with the research team for documentation.
The tourism office said original materials may be brought or submitted temporarily for documentation.

Those who wish to contribute may contact the Lubang Tourism, Culture and Arts Office or email lubangtourism@gmail.com. They may also contact Tourism Officer Gina Tabor-Julaton through 0998-996-2878 or Facebook Messenger.

The municipal government appealed particularly to senior citizens, former Balsehan performers, musicians, choreographers, cultural practitioners and people who witnessed or participated in the tradition to share their memories.
It said their firsthand accounts are vital to building a more accurate and community-based record of the Balsehan ng Lubang for future generations. INQ

articles.title: Bigger allocation for AFP modernization pushed
articles.summary: CALAPAN CITY, Oriental Mindoro — House Deputy Majority Leader Arnan Panaligan pressed defense officials to ensure adequate, timely and sustainable funding for the Armed Forces of the Philippines…

blocks.text: CALAPAN CITY, Oriental Mindoro — House Deputy Majority Leader Arnan Panaligan pressed defense officials to ensure adequate, timely and sustainable funding for the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) Modernization Program.
He made the move during the recent budget briefing of the House Committee on Appropriations last week.
Panaligan, who is the Oriental Mindoro congressman, also advocated legislative fixes to loan limits and funding gaps that can delay critical defense acquisitions.
During the interpellation of National Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro on August 25, the lawmaker highlighted key issues surrounding the program’s financing.
These include the release of unspent funds to the need for expanded borrowing authority and clearer spending priorities.
The proposed 2027 national budget allocates P50 billion for AFP modernization under a Multi-Year Contractual Authority (MYCA) intended to support long-term defense acquisition contracts.
Meanwhile, the P50 billion in unprogrammed appropriations earmarked for the program in the 2026 budget has yet to be released.

Budget Secretary Kim Robert de Leon earlier told the committee that the funds would be made available only upon request from the Department of National Defense and AFP, subject to the availability of excess revenues.
He also said that the allocation will be given only after the ₱40 billion regular appropriation for 2026 is fully utilized.

“We requested the DND to submit a detailed update on how the ₱40 billion has been spent, including specific items funded under it, as well as the priority acquisitions to be charged to the proposed ₱50 billion for 2027,” Panaligan said on Monday.

blocks.text: CITY OF SAN FERNANDO, Pampanga — Rescuers recovered on Aug. 31 the body of a 9-year-old boy who was swept away by strong currents in Guagua town three days earlier.

The Grade 2 student slipped from a concrete slope protection along a river in Barangay San Jose, Guagua, on Aug. 29 while accompanying a still-unidentified man who had gone fishing, according to the Guagua Information Office.
Strong currents carried the boy downstream to Barangay Santa Monica in neighboring Lubao town, where rescuers recovered his body on Monday.
The incident came amid heavy monsoon rains that caused widespread flooding in parts of Pampanga. /mcm

articles.title: Duped on confidential funds? Prosecution spoxes say DepEd under VP Sara pulled a fast one on AFP
articles.summary: The Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) was allegedly "duped" into issuing certifications that were later used by the Department of Education (DepEd) under then-secretary, Vice President Sara…

blocks.text: The Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) was allegedly "duped" into issuing certifications that were later used by the Department of Education (DepEd) under then-secretary, Vice President Sara Duterte to help justify the liquidation of P15.54 million in confidential funds, House prosecutors said Tuesday.

House prosecution panel layman spokespersons Lanao del Sur 1st district Rep. Zia Alonto Adiong and Robert Ace Barbers had this to say during day 20 of Duterte’s Senate impeachment trial, which featured the testimony of Col. Manaros Boransing II.
“Isa lang po ang puwedeng ma-draw as a conclusion from the testimony of Colonel Boransing: nabudol po ang AFP,” Adiong said in no uncertain terms.
(Only one conclusion can be drawn from Colonel Boransing’s testimony: the AFP was duped.)

Boransing testified that his Jan. 1, 2024 certification to DepEd--as presented before senator-judges Tuesday--covered eight Youth Leadership Summits (YLS) and 53 Information Education Campaign (IEC) activities conducted by the 1st Infantry “Tabak” Division with other stakeholders in 2023.

He also testified that no DepEd money was released or downloaded to his division for the activities. He said he understood the document as a routine certification of participation, and only learned during an October 2024 House probe that DepEd had used it in responding to the Commission on Audit's (COA) findings on the agency’s confidential funds.
“Nabudol ang AFP dahil hiningan sila ng certification na ang paggamit noon ay i-justify nila sa COA,” Adiong said.
(The AFP was duped because they were asked for a certification that was later used to justify [the expenditure] before the COA.)

DepEd attached the Army certifications to its April 17, 2024 response to COA Audit Observation Memorandum No. 2024-015, which sought records supporting rewards totaling P15.54 million for the reported success of information-gathering or surveillance activities.
Adiong said the certifications could only establish that the activities took place, not that confidential funds were spent on them.

“The certificate only proves that there was a summit that was conducted. There was such an event that happened on that particular date. It did not prove anything as to the utilization of confidential funds. It did not prove anything that the reward was made during that event."
Likewise, Barbers underscored that the AFP certifications were obtained without the issuing officers knowing how they would eventually be used.

“The AFP was duped. Its certifications were obtained, but the officers who issued them did not even know that their documents would later be used to support the liquidation of P15 million in confidential funds,” Barbers said.

Former DepEd Undersecretary Michael Poa had acknowledged requesting then-undersecretary Nolasco Mempin to secure military certifications in connection with the liquidation of the confidential-fund expenditure.

“You cannot use an AFP certification to prove that money was spent when the AFP did not receive the money, did not spend the money, and did not know its certification would be used as proof of the expenditure,” stressed the former three-term Surigao del Norte representative.
Up to court to decide

Barbers said the impeachment court would ultimately determine whether or not the episode resulted from gross negligence or was part of a deliberate scheme to create a paper trail for the P15.54-million expenditure.
“If the AFP itself says it did not fund these activities and did not know why its certifications were being secured, then what exactly were those certifications supposed to clear?” Barbers asked.
“The documents may carry official seals and signatures, but those signatures do not magically turn an unsupported expenditure into a legitimate one,” he further said.
